UNIT.subject: Core Mathematics
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
UNIT.content:
• Surface area of prisms (triangular, rectangular, and other prisms)
• Surface area of pyramids (square-based and other pyramids)
• Surface area of cones
• Surface area of frustums (cone frustums)
• Surface area of spheres
• Surface area of composite solids
• Volume of prisms (triangular, rectangular, and other prisms)
• Volume of pyramids (square-based and other pyramids)
• Volume of cones
• Volume of frustums
• Volume of spheres
• Volume of composite solids
• Real-life applications of surface area and volume of solids
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) determine the surface area of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres,
b) determine the surface area of composite solids,
c) determine the volume of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres,
d) determine the volume of composite solids,
e) apply surface area and volume of solids to real-life situations,
f) appreciate the use of surface area and volume of solids in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner discusses and shares findings with peers when measuring and calculating the surface area and volume of locally available solid models such as tins, packets and containers used for ugali flour or cooking oil.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner analyses composite solid shapes found in real-life Kenyan contexts — such as grain silos in Eldoret or water tanks in rural Rift Valley — and decomposes them to determine total surface area and volume.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner improvises and constructs nets and models of prisms, pyramids, cones and spheres using locally available materials (cardboard, manila paper) to verify surface area formulae.
• Digital Literacy: the learner uses digital devices and software (where available) to explore 3D solid models, nets and volume visualisations.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner builds confidence in applying surface area and volume formulae independently to solve real-world packaging, construction and storage problems relevant to Kenyan industries.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: the learner carefully handles models of solids and measurement tools collected from the immediate environment, and accurately records measurements to ensure correct calculations of surface area and volume.
• Integrity: the learner applies formulae with accurate measurements and honest working, adhering to mathematical rigour when solving surface area and volume problems.
• Unity: the learner works collaboratively in groups to construct solid models, measure dimensions and verify calculated surface areas and volumes, appreciating each member's contribution.
• Respect: the learner recognises and values the input of every group member during practical activities involving the construction and measurement of solid models.
UNIT.sep:
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: learners apply and manipulate formulae for surface area and volume of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums, spheres and composite solids, using arithmetic and algebraic reasoning to solve quantitative problems.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: learners plan and conduct hands-on measurement investigations using real solid objects (tins, boxes, cones) to collect dimension data, then compute and compare calculated surface area and volume against estimates.
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: learners examine measured dimensions and computed results, identify errors or inconsistencies, and draw conclusions about which solid shape optimises volume for a given surface area — relevant to packaging and storage design.
• Constructing Explanations: learners construct clear mathematical explanations of how surface area and volume formulae are derived from nets and cross-sectional areas, and explain results in context (e.g. why a cylindrical water tank in Kisumu holds more than a box of the same surface area).
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: learners present their findings on surface area and volume of composite solids to the class, evaluating the reasonableness of results and communicating solution strategies clearly.
UNIT.pcis:
• Education for Sustainable Development (Environmental Education): the learner uses and repurposes locally available materials such as cardboard packaging, tin cans and plastic containers to construct solid models, promoting environmental consciousness and waste reduction.
• Social Cohesion: the learner works in groups to build models, measure solids and solve problems, fostering teamwork and mutual respect across diverse learner backgrounds.
• Socio-Economic Issues: the learner applies surface area and volume concepts to real Kenyan economic contexts such as determining the amount of metal sheet needed to fabricate a water tank in Nakuru, or the capacity of a grain store in the Rift Valley, linking mathematics to livelihoods and national development.
• Home Science and Technology: the learner connects volume calculations to everyday household decisions such as estimating the volume of a sufuria used for cooking ugali or the capacity of a storage jerrycan.
UNIT.careers:
• Architecture and Civil Engineering: understanding surface area informs material estimation for roofing, wall cladding and flooring of buildings — directly relevant to Kenya's affordable housing programmes.
• Manufacturing and Packaging Industry: volume and surface area calculations are essential for designing and optimising packaging for Kenyan food products such as maize flour, cooking oil and tea from Kericho.
• Water and Sanitation Engineering: volume of cylinders, frustums and spheres is applied in designing water storage tanks, pipes and reservoirs for communities around Lake Victoria and arid regions.
• Agriculture and Agribusiness: farmers in the Rift Valley and Central Kenya use volume concepts to estimate grain storage capacity in cylindrical silos and conical heaps.
• Medicine and Pharmacy: volume of spherical capsules and cylindrical vials is critical in drug dosage calculations and medical device manufacturing.
• Surveying and Land Management: surface area concepts underpin calculations of land volumes in road construction and mining operations in regions such as Taita Hills.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to calculate the surface area and volume of common solids — prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums, spheres and composite solids — grounding every formula in the physical reality of objects found in Kenyan daily life (grain tins, water tanks, roofing cones, sports balls). Learners move from hands-on net construction and measurement of real objects to formal derivation and application of formulae, building both procedural fluency and conceptual understanding. The unit culminates in a real-life project where learners design or evaluate a practical solid structure (e.g. a water storage tank or grain silo) relevant to their local community, integrating surface area and volume to make informed decisions.
UNIT.phenomenon: A local posho mill owner in Eldoret has two large metal storage containers for holding maize grain: one is a tall cylindrical drum and the other is a rectangular metal box. Both containers appear roughly the same size from the outside, and the metalsmith who made them used the same total area of iron sheet for each. Yet when grain is poured in, the cylindrical drum holds noticeably more maize than the rectangular box. The mill owner is puzzled — if the same amount of metal was used for both, why does one hold more grain? Students observe photographs and physical models of both containers, measure their dimensions, and are challenged to explain the discrepancy. This phenomenon is puzzling because learners intuitively assume equal surface area means equal volume, but discover that shape — not just material used — determines storage capacity, launching an investigation into how surface area and volume are related yet distinct properties of three-dimensional solids.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A mandazi vendor in Mombasa notices that ball-shaped (spherical) mandazi cool down more slowly than flat disc-shaped ones of the same mass — prompting investigation into how surface area relative to volume affects heat loss and connects to the surface area of spheres.
• A water harvesting project in Turkana County must choose between a conical, cylindrical and hemispherical roof-catchment tank; all use the same amount of plastic sheeting — students investigate which shape stores the most water, exploring volume and surface area of cones, cylinders and spheres.
• Workers at a Nairobi packaging factory notice that when a conical top is placed on a cylindrical can (like a composite solid), the total surface area to be painted changes in a non-obvious way — prompting learners to decompose composite solids and calculate total surface areas systematically.
• A school in Kisumu receives a donation of spherical footballs and asks: how much leather (surface area) is needed to make each ball, and how much air (volume) does it hold? — anchoring the surface area and volume of spheres in a familiar, motivating context.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain — and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids?
2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Anchoring Phenomenon & Surface Area of Prisms: Learners observe the anchoring phenomenon (two containers, same metal sheet, different grain capacity). They predict which holds more and why. They construct nets of rectangular and triangular prisms from cardboard, measure faces, and derive the surface area formula. They calculate the surface area of the rectangular box from the phenomenon and record findings on the Driving Question Board (DQB).

Lesson 2 — Surface Area of Pyramids: Learners examine pyramid-roofed structures common in Kenyan homesteads (e.g. traditional Maasai manyatta roofs and school hall rooftops). They construct nets of square-based and triangular pyramids, identify slant height versus vertical height, and derive the surface area formula. They solve problems involving material needed to cover a pyramid-shaped roof.

Lesson 3 — Surface Area of Cones and Frustums: Learners investigate the cone shape using real objects (ice-cream cones, conical grain heaps, funnel tops of water tanks). They derive the curved surface area formula using the net of a cone (a sector of a circle). They extend this to the frustum by considering a cone with its top removed, linking to the Turkana water-tank supporting phenomenon. Learners calculate the metal sheet needed for a conical tank top.

Lesson 4 — Surface Area of Spheres and Composite Solids: Learners explore the surface area of spheres by wrapping a ball in paper strips, then verify using the formula SA = 4πr². They extend to composite solids (cylinder + cone; hemisphere + cylinder) and practise decomposing shapes. They connect to the Nairobi packaging factory supporting phenomenon and the football supporting phenomenon. The DQB is updated with new understanding.

Lesson 5 — Volume of Prisms and Pyramids: Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon and now investigate volume. They fill rectangular and triangular prism models with sand or water and compare. They derive Volume = base area × height for prisms and V = ⅓ × base area × height for pyramids by comparing filled models. They compute the volume of the rectangular box from Lesson 1 and compare it with the cylinder (previewing Lesson 6).

Lesson 6 — Volume of Cones, Frustums and Spheres: Learners use the relationship between cone and cylinder volumes (V_cone = ⅓ V_cylinder) demonstrated by pouring water between matching models. They derive V = ⅓πr²h for cones and V = 4/3πr³ for spheres. They calculate the volume of the cylindrical drum from the anchoring phenomenon and formally resolve why it holds more grain than the rectangular box of equal surface area.

Lesson 7 — Volume and Surface Area of Composite Solids & Real-Life Applications: Learners tackle multi-step problems involving composite solids such as a cylindrical water tank with a hemispherical top (common in Kenyan water projects). They calculate both the total surface area (painting/material cost) and volume (water storage capacity). They also work on a grain silo problem set in the Rift Valley, integrating all formulae learned.

Lesson 8 — Project Presentations, Model Building & Unit Consolidation: Learner groups present their home/extended project: designing a storage container (grain silo, water tank or cooking pot) for a Kenyan community need, specifying dimensions, total surface area of material required and volume/capacity. Groups critique each other's designs. The class builds a final cumulative model on the DQB linking surface area and volume formulae to the anchoring phenomenon, resolving the driving question fully and discussing careers that use these concepts.

LESSONS.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Surface Area of Prisms: Same Metal, Different Grain
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; the rectangular-prism net and the 3-4-5 triangular prism net are done in pairs)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: surface area, net, prism, face, base area, perimeter, total surface area, volume, capacity, Driving Question Board, posho mill, Eldoret

slo.purpose: Launch the anchoring phenomenon (Mzee Kiplagat's two containers made from the same 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet but holding different amounts of maize) and build the first idea needed to explain it: the surface area of a prism is the sum of the areas of the faces in its net, which equals 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) draw and cut out the net of a rectangular prism and of a triangular prism; (2) find the total surface area (TSA) of a prism by adding the areas of all faces in its net; (3) use TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length; (4) calculate the TSA of the rectangular box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) as 30,800 cm2; (5) state that surface area (material covering a solid) and volume (space inside) are different quantities. KICD outcome addressed: determine the surface area of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums, spheres and composite solids. KICD Key Inquiry Question 1: How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids?
slo.skills: Developing and using models (nets and physical prism models); asking questions and defining problems (DQB); analysing and interpreting data (measuring faces, tabulating areas); using mathematics (calculating areas of rectangles and triangles); constructing explanations and arguing from evidence. KICD core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (learners compare the two containers and test the idea that equal material means equal capacity); Communication and Collaboration (learners share measurements and reasoning in pairs and with the class); Creativity and Imagination (learners build nets from cardboard).
slo.attitudes: KICD values: Responsibility (learners take care of cardboard, scissors and measuring tools and return them); Integrity (learners record measurements honestly and accurately, as Wanjiru the metalsmith did by measuring and not guessing); Unity (learners work in pairs and respect each other's ideas). PCI: Education for Sustainable Development (learners reuse waste cardboard and cut with minimal wastage, like a metal fabricator who wastes no sheet).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations? Lesson focus: If two containers use exactly the same amount of metal, must they hold the same amount of maize?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson. It introduces the phenomenon and opens the DQB. It gives learners the sum-of-faces method (nets) for surface area and the box's TSA of 30,800 cm2. Lesson 2 builds on nets and the sum-of-faces method for pyramids. Comparing volumes is left for Lessons 5 and 6, so learners leave this lesson knowing the box's SA but still puzzled about why the drum holds more.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors: cut away from the body, pass handles-first, and keep scissors on the desk when not cutting. Use blunt-tip scissors or a razor-free cutting method only. Do not use blades. Keep floors clear of cardboard offcuts to prevent slipping. Do not bring real metal drums to class; use photographs and small models. If using a real jerrican or tin, check for sharp edges first.

LESSONS.overview: Learners meet Mzee Kiplagat, who owns a posho mill in Eldoret. He asked Wanjiru, a jua kali metalsmith, to make two closed storage containers for maize: a cylindrical drum and a square-based rectangular box, each from exactly 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet. Both stand about 1 m tall and look about the same size, yet the drum holds more maize. Learners first predict which holds more and why, then investigate surface area by making nets of a 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm rectangular prism and a triangular prism with 3-4-5 cm right-angled triangle ends and length 10 cm. They add the face areas, discover that TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter x length, and apply it to the box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) to find 30,800 cm2. They then record what they have learned and what they still wonder on the Driving Question Board (DQB). They leave with the box's surface area confirmed but the puzzle of the drum still open, since the drum's SA and the volumes are investigated in later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners view a photograph or poster of Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret showing the tall cylindrical drum and the square-based rectangular box side by side. The teacher reads the story aloud: Wanjiru, the jua kali metalsmith, used exactly 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet for each closed container, and both stand about 1 m tall. Individually (2 minutes) learners write on a prediction slip: (a) Which container will hold more maize, or will they hold the same? (b) Why do you think so? They draw a quick sketch of each container. They then share with a partner (2 minutes) and record a class tally of predictions on the board: drum holds more, box holds more, same. Learners are told only that the owner found that the two do not hold the same amount; the result is not revealed in detail yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the photograph and say: 'Mzee Kiplagat is puzzled. Wanjiru used exactly the same amount of iron sheet, 30,800 cm2, for each container. Do you think they hold the same amount of maize?' Then give 2 minutes of silent writing. Say: 'Write your prediction and your reason. There is no wrong answer today; I want to see your thinking.' Move around and note, without commenting, which learners write 'same material, so same amount'. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before taking responses. Cold-call 3 learners with different predictions: 'Wanjiru, what did you predict and what is your reason?' After each answer ask a different learner: 'Who can restate that idea in your own words?' Do not confirm or correct. Say: 'Keep your slip safe. We will come back to it at the end.' Tally the predictions on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning and public tallying (eliciting prior ideas). Writing a prediction and a reason makes learners commit to the common intuition that equal material means equal capacity. The class tally makes the disagreement visible, so the puzzle becomes a shared problem and gives a reason to investigate. It also allows the teacher to see how many hold the misconception that surface area and volume are the same thing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and record: (1) number of learners who predicted 'the same' and gave the reason 'same sheet metal' (indicates the surface area = volume misconception); (2) whether learners distinguish material used (surface) from amount held (inside); (3) whether at least 8 of 10 learners complete both parts (a) and (b) of the prediction slip with a reason. Collect slips from 5 randomly chosen learners to compare with the end-of-lesson revision.

framework.learnerExperience: In pairs, learners observe and measure physical prism models and build nets. Task A (rectangular prism): measure a 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm cardboard box (or make one), unfold it flat, or draw and cut out its net from cardboard, labelling each face with its dimensions. They identify that there are 6 rectangular faces in 3 equal pairs: 5 x 4 = 20 cm2 (two), 5 x 3 = 15 cm2 (two), 4 x 3 = 12 cm2 (two). They add to get TSA = 2(20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm2. Task B (triangular prism): make or examine a prism with right-angled triangle ends 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm and length 10 cm. They draw its net: 2 triangles (each 1/2 x 3 x 4 = 6 cm2) and 3 rectangles (3 x 10 = 30, 4 x 10 = 40, 5 x 10 = 50, which total 120 cm2). TSA = 12 + 120 = 132 cm2. They record results in a table with columns: Face, Shape, Dimensions, Area (cm2). Then they look at both tables and look for a pattern linking the two ends (bases) and the rectangles around them.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute pre-cut cardboard (reuse old cereal and soap cartons), rulers, pencils and blunt-tip scissors to each pair. Say: 'Wanjiru did not guess. She measured, and she worked with flat pieces of sheet. Today you will do the same: unfold the solid into a flat net and measure every face.' Remind learners of the safety rule: 'Scissors point down and away from you.' Circulate and ask: 'How many faces does your prism have? Which faces are identical? How do you know?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before accepting answers. Prompt pairs who finish early: 'The two triangles in the net are the bases. What is the total length of the rectangles laid side by side, and how does it compare with the perimeter of the triangle?' Cold-call 2 pairs to report their TSA for each prism: 'Pair at the window, what is your total for the rectangular prism? Pair at the back, what did you get for the triangular prism?' Confirm 94 cm2 and 132 cm2 only after the evidence is shared. Draw the table on the board and fill it with learners' values.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with physical nets and data tables (Developing and using models). Unfolding a 3D prism into a flat net lets learners see every face at once, so no face is missed or counted twice. The data table organises the areas, and comparing the two prisms helps learners notice the structure: two identical ends plus a set of rectangles that wrap around. This pattern-finding is the basis for the general formula in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each pair's net and table. Indicators: (1) the rectangular prism net has 6 faces labelled with correct areas 20, 20, 15, 15, 12, 12 cm2; (2) the triangular prism net shows 2 triangles of 6 cm2 and 3 rectangles of 30, 40, 50 cm2; (3) totals of 94 cm2 and 132 cm2 are correct; (4) the learner can say that the rectangles' widths together equal the perimeter of the triangle (3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm). Mark pairs who forgot the second triangle or the second set of faces and re-ask the guiding question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their tables to generalise. In pairs they answer: What do the two bases contribute? (2 x base area) What do the rectangles around the base contribute? (together they form one long rectangle of length = perimeter of base and width = length of the prism). They write: TSA of a prism = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length. They check the formula on the 5 x 4 x 3 prism (taking 5 x 4 as the base: 2 x 20 + 18 x 3 = 40 + 54 = 94 cm2) and on the 3-4-5 prism (2 x 6 + 12 x 10 = 132 cm2). They then apply it to Mzee Kiplagat's box: square base 50 cm x 50 cm, height 129 cm (the length of this prism). Base area = 2,500 cm2, so 2 x base = 5,000 cm2. Perimeter = 200 cm, so 200 x 129 = 25,800 cm2. TSA = 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2, the same 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet that Wanjiru used. Learners also sketch the net of the box. Finally they write one sentence distinguishing surface area (the material covering the outside) from volume (the space inside), and record that the box's volume has not been found yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your two tables. What stays the same in both? What changes?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to describe the pattern in their own words. Build the formula on the board from learner responses, not by telling: 'Two bases, plus the rectangles that wrap around. If I lay the rectangles side by side, how long is that strip?' Write TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter x length. Ask: 'Why does perimeter appear in the formula?' Cold-call 2 learners. Then pose the key task: 'Mzee Kiplagat's box is 50 cm by 50 cm by 129 cm. Use the formula to find how much sheet Wanjiru needed.' Let pairs work for 4 minutes, then cold-call 2 pairs to show the steps. Confirm 30,800 cm2 and say: 'This matches the amount of iron sheet Wanjiru used. So the maths agrees with the real workshop.' Address the misconception: 'We found how much material covers the box. Have we found how much maize it holds? Not yet. Surface area and volume are different quantities.' Do not teach the drum's SA or any volume formula today.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern generalisation from data followed by application to the anchor (claim-evidence-reasoning). Learners derive the formula from their own measurements, test it on two prisms (evidence), and then use it on the real container (application). Linking the result to Wanjiru's 30,800 cm2 validates the mathematics against the phenomenon. Explicitly separating 'covering' from 'holding' prepares learners to see why equal surface area does not guarantee equal volume.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners write TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter x length correctly; (2) they identify the base of the box as 50 x 50 and the length as 129 cm; (3) they calculate 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2 with the unit cm2; (4) they can explain in one sentence why perimeter x length gives the area of the rectangles around the base; (5) they distinguish surface area from volume in writing. Use a 3-question exit check on mini-whiteboards: (a) TSA of a 6 cm x 5 cm x 2 cm prism (base 6 x 5: 2 x 30 + 22 x 2 = 104 cm2); (b) 'Does the box's TSA tell us how much maize it holds? Yes or no, and why?'; (c) 'Which unit do we use for surface area?' Aim for at least 80% correct; revisit the formula with those who did not reach it.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher displays the driving question on a large chart: 'Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain, and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?' Learners individually write at least one question on sticky notes or paper strips about the phenomenon (for example: How much does the drum hold? What is the drum's surface area? How do we find the volume of a cylinder? Is there a shape that holds the most? Why would a round container be better?). In groups of four they sort their questions into categories such as Surface area questions, Volume questions, and Shape and design questions, and post them on the DQB. Beside the board they add a small 'What we know so far' panel: the box's TSA is 30,800 cm2; TSA of a prism = 2 x base area + perimeter x length; surface area is not the same as volume.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Scientists and engineers begin with questions. What are you still wondering about Mzee Kiplagat's containers?' Give 3 minutes of silent writing and then use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups sort. Circulate and push for deeper questions: 'Can you turn that into a question we can investigate with measurements?' Cold-call 4 learners to read one question each and place it on the board with a reason for its category. Highlight questions that match upcoming lessons, for example: 'Wekesa asks how to find the drum's surface area. We will investigate curved surfaces later in this unit.' Do not answer volume questions now; say: 'Good question. Let us keep it on the board and come back with evidence.' Point to the KICD key inquiry questions and link them to learners' questions. Keep the DQB visible for all remaining lessons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (student-generated questions). The DQB gives learners ownership of the unit's direction and keeps the phenomenon at the centre. Sorting questions into categories shows how the lessons connect, and the 'What we know so far' panel records the first piece of evidence (box TSA = 30,800 cm2) so progress is visible across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) every learner contributes at least one question; (2) at least 3 groups include a question about volume or capacity, which shows they recognise that volume is a separate idea; (3) at least 2 questions ask about the drum or about shape (for example, why round?), showing connection to the phenomenon; (4) learners place questions in sensible categories and justify their choice. Photograph or copy the DQB so questions can be compared at the end of the unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners start the class's first version of the explanatory model on a chart titled 'Why does the drum hold more maize?'. Individually they sketch the two containers (drum and box) with labels: both closed, both 30,800 cm2 of sheet. Under the box they write the dimensions 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm and 'TSA = 30,800 cm2'. Under the drum they write the dimensions r = 35 cm and h = 105 cm and a question mark for TSA and volume, because these are not yet calculated. They add an arrow labelled 'material that covers = surface area' and another labelled 'space inside = volume' and write a first explanation in their own words, for example: 'Surface area tells how much sheet is used. Volume tells how much maize it holds. We need to compare them.' Learners revisit their prediction slips, put a tick or a cross, and write one sentence about whether their thinking has changed. They complete the summary table (see below) in their books.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Today your model is a first draft. We will keep adding to it in every lesson until we can explain why the drum holds more.' Give learners 5 minutes to draw and write, then use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 3 learners to read their one-sentence explanation. Ask: 'What do we know for certain? What do we still need to find?' (We know the box's TSA is 30,800 cm2; we need the drum's SA, and both volumes.) Ask learners to hand in or keep their models in their folders. Give the closing prompt: 'Next lesson we will look at roofs on a school hall in Kajiado and learn how to find surface area when the faces are triangles that slope. As you walk home, look at a water tank or a sufuria and ask yourself: is it the covering or the contents that matters?' Remind them to return all scissors and cardboard offcuts to the collection box.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building (initial model with open questions). Drawing the two containers with known and unknown values shows exactly what has been established and what remains. Writing the distinction between surface area and volume in the model makes the central idea explicit, and revising the earlier prediction shows learners how their thinking has grown. The model will be revised after each lesson, ending in Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: (1) both containers drawn with correct dimensions (drum r = 35 cm, h = 105 cm; box 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm); (2) box TSA written as 30,800 cm2 with the correct unit; (3) surface area and volume labelled as different quantities; (4) at least one open question about the drum or volume; (5) a revised prediction sentence. Learners who still say 'same sheet, so same maize' should be seen in the next lesson's starter. Record the number of learners meeting 4 or more of the 5 indicators.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) How many learners still believed at the end that equal surface area means equal capacity, and what evidence from the prediction slips and models shows this? (2) Did all pairs build both nets correctly, and which faces were most often missed (usually the second base or the second set of rectangles)? (3) Could learners explain in their own words why perimeter x length gives the area of the rectangles around the base? (4) Did the DQB produce questions about volume and about shape, and did I protect those questions from being answered too early? (5) Which learners need extra support with area of rectangles and triangles from Grade 9 before Lesson 2? (6) Were materials, such as cardboard and scissors, sufficient and safely used? Plan adjustments for the next lesson, for example a quick starter on Pythagoras and slant height.

summaryTablePrompt.learned: The total surface area of a prism is the sum of the areas of all the faces in its net: TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length. The box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) has TSA = 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2. Surface area measures the material covering a solid, and volume measures the space inside, so they are different quantities.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Wanjiru used 30,800 cm2 of sheet for the box, which agrees with our calculation, so the same amount of material is used for both containers. But knowing the surface area does not tell us how much maize a container holds, because capacity depends on volume. We still need to find the drum's surface area and both volumes to explain why the drum holds more; this is now on our DQB.

LESSONS.title: Surface Area of Pyramids: Slant Height, Vertical Height and Roof Cover
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: pyramid, slant height, vertical height, net, triangular face, base area, roof area, tetrahedron, Pythagoras, total surface area, curved surface, Wanjiru, Mzee Kiplagat

slo.purpose: Learners build on Lesson 1 (nets and the sum-of-faces method for prisms) to find the surface area of pyramids, and they distinguish slant height (l) from vertical height (h). This advances the driving question by showing that Wanjiru, the jua kali metalsmith, must use the correct measurement (slant height, not vertical height) to calculate the sheet or roofing material a solid needs. It also shows that surface area measures covering material only.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) distinguish the slant height (l) of a pyramid from its vertical height (h); (b) use Pythagoras' theorem to find l from h and half the base side (3² + 4² = 5²); (c) state and apply pyramid TSA = base area + sum of the areas of the triangular faces; (d) calculate the roof area of a square-based pyramid roof (6 m base, h = 4 m, l = 5 m, roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2) and the surface area of a regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron, all edges 6 cm, each face 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2, TSA ≈ 62.35 cm2).
slo.skills: Constructing and folding nets (Developing and Using Models); measuring and labelling; applying Pythagoras' theorem; analysing and interpreting data (comparing measurements of h and l); using mathematics and computational thinking; constructing explanations; communicating and collaborating in groups; critical thinking and problem solving.
slo.attitudes: Responsibility: learners take care of the materials and use cut-outs from the immediate environment carefully. Integrity: learners measure and record accurately and report their true measurements. Unity: learners work together to build the nets and share their ideas. Appreciation of how mathematics is used in construction and roofing in Kenya.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the Eldoret phenomenon: the drum and the box both use 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet, and the box's SA was found with nets and the sum-of-faces method. Lesson 2 extends the same net idea to pyramids. It introduces slant height, which Lesson 3 will need for cones and frustums, and it reinforces that surface area is only the covering material, so it cannot tell us how much a solid holds. That prepares learners for the volume lessons (L5 and L6) that resolve why the drum holds more maize than the box.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors and craft knives: cut away from the body and keep fingers clear of the blade. Do not climb onto any real roof or structure; take all measurements from models, photographs and the diagram. Keep the floor clear of paper offcuts to prevent slips. Do not leave scissors on the edges of desks. Use blunt-tipped scissors where possible.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kiplagat has since asked Wanjiru to roof a small store at his posho mill with a pyramid-shaped iron-sheet roof, just like the school hall roofs and Maasai manyatta-style roofs seen in Kajiado and Narok. Learners first predict how much roofing sheet a 6 m x 6 m pyramid roof with a vertical height of 4 m will need. They then construct nets of a square-based pyramid and a regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron), measure and compare vertical height with slant height, and use Pythagoras to find l = 5 m. They derive that pyramid TSA = base area + areas of the triangular faces, and calculate that the roof area is 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2 (the triangular faces only, since a roof has no floor). A tetrahedron with edges of 6 cm gives about 62.35 cm2. Learners revisit the Driving Question Board and add pyramid evidence to the class model: surface area is the covering material needed, found by adding the face areas, and it is a different quantity from volume.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at photographs of a Maasai manyatta roof from Narok and a school hall roof in Kajiado. Mzee Kiplagat wants Wanjiru to roof his store with a square-based pyramid roof with a 6 m x 6 m base and a vertical height of 4 m. In pairs, learners individually write then share a prediction: How many m2 of iron sheet will cover the four sloping faces? They also say which length of the roof they would use for the height of one triangular face, and why. Some will predict 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 4 = 48 m2 using the vertical height; others will guess something else. Learners record their prediction in their books, with a reason, and draw a quick sketch of the roof showing the length they think they need. They link this back to Lesson 1: 'we found the SA of the box by adding the faces, so can we do the same here?'
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two photographs and say: 'Wanjiru has to buy iron sheet for this roof. Before we learn anything new, what do you think she needs to know?' Give individual silent think time and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks. Then ask learners to turn to a partner for 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 pairs to share their predictions, and write each one on the board without judging it. Ask: 'Which length did you use for the height of a triangular face, and why?' Ask: 'What did we do in Lesson 1 to find the surface area of the box, and could that help here?' Do not say whether any prediction is correct. Keep the predictions displayed for later comparison. Then ask the whole class: 'Do we expect the roof to need as much sheet as the drum or box used?' to link it back to 30,800 cm2.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Prediction) with Think-Pair-Share: Recording a prediction and a reason before instruction exposes learners' ideas (for instance, that vertical height can be used for the triangular face). When learners later compare their prediction with evidence, they experience a conflict that motivates the idea of slant height, and they own the correction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) how many learners use the vertical height of 4 m in their calculation, a sign of the slant-height misconception, and tally them on the board; (2) whether learners suggest adding the areas of the faces, which shows transfer from Lesson 1; (3) whether any learners confuse 'area of the roof' with 'space inside the roof' (volume). Record the numbers of each type of response. Use a thumbs-up/down check for 'Is it possible to know the roof area without measuring a sloping edge?'

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners use a pre-drawn net (or draw their own on manila paper or old cartons) to build two models: (A) a square-based pyramid with a 6 cm square base and four triangular faces (scale model of the 6 m roof, where 1 cm = 1 m, vertical height 4 cm), and (B) a regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron) with all edges 6 cm. Learners cut, fold and tape the nets. For model A, they first draw the net, measure a triangular face, and then measure the vertical height (from the apex straight down to the centre of the base) with a ruler and a straight stick, and the slant height (from the apex down the middle of a triangular face to the midpoint of a base edge). They record h = 4 and l = 5 (scale units) and check that 3² + 4² = 5² (the right-angled triangle formed by the vertical height, half the base side, and the slant height). They then calculate the area of one triangular face (1/2 x 6 x 5 = 15), then four faces (60). For model B, they measure the base side (6 cm) and the height of one face (about 5.2 cm), and compute each face as 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2. Groups record their measurements in a table with columns: solid, base, h, l, area of one face, number of faces, total.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute nets, rulers, scissors, tape and sticks. Say: 'Your job is to find the length that Wanjiru must use for the height of each triangular face. Measure, do not guess.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which line is the vertical height and which is the slant height? Show me with your finger on the model.' Hold up a model and say: 'Where does the slant height touch the base?' Pose the challenge: 'Why is the slant height longer than the vertical height?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Prompt with: 'Which right-angled triangle can you see inside the pyramid? What are its three sides?' Remind learners about safety with scissors. Remind learners that, as in Lesson 1, the net shows every face laid flat. Do not give the formula yet. Ask groups to put away their tapes only after they have recorded the data. Then ask: 'Is the base counted if this is a roof?' and 'Is it counted if we were making a closed pyramid-shaped container?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model-based investigation with data table (Developing and Using Models; Analysing Data): Building the physical model and measuring both h and l from the same solid makes the difference visible and concrete. Organising results in a table lets learners see patterns (area of one face x number of faces) before they are given a formula, building understanding from evidence rather than from rote.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the learner can point to the vertical height inside the pyramid and to the slant height along a face and say why they differ; (2) the learner measures l along the face, not along the edge of the pyramid; (3) the learner records l = 5 for model A and checks it with 3² + 4² = 5²; (4) the learner calculates a single triangular face area using l as the height of the triangle. Use a checklist of these four items for each group. Intervene if a group uses the edge length instead of slant height, and ask them to compare with a right-angled triangle drawn on the net.

framework.learnerExperience: Using their measurements, learners explain to their groups and then to the class: (1) why the height of each triangular face is the slant height l and not the vertical height h; (2) how to find l when only h and the base side are known, using Pythagoras: l² = h² + (half the base)² = 4² + 3² = 25, so l = 5 m; (3) how to derive the formula. They fill in the sentence frame: 'Pyramid TSA = base area + the sum of the areas of the triangular faces.' For the roof, they decide that the base (the floor of the store) is not covered with iron sheet, so the roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2, while the closed-pyramid TSA would be 36 + 60 = 96 m2. For the tetrahedron, they calculate each face as 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2 and the TSA as 4 x 15.59 ≈ 62.35 cm2. Learners then solve a new problem: a pyramid-shaped roof for a school hall in Kajiado with a 8 m x 8 m base and a vertical height of 3 m; find l = 5 m, roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 8 x 5 = 80 m2. Learners write a short statement correcting their earlier prediction and say what the answer of 60 m2 tells us about the material needed, and what it does not tell us (how much space is inside the roof).
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Using what you measured, why can't we use 4 m as the height of the triangle?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners, and push for evidence: 'What did you measure that shows this?' Draw the right-angled triangle (h = 4, half-base = 3, l = 5) on the board and have learners come up and label it. Say: 'Slant height is never called height. We write l for slant and h for vertical.' Introduce the formula only after learners propose it in their own words. Work the 60 m2 example on the board with learners calling out each step, then have them solve the 8 m x 8 m, h = 3 m school hall roof in pairs. Cold-call 4 pairs for l, a face area, and the total. Return to the Predict phase: 'Whose prediction was closest? What was the error in the 48 m2 prediction?' Ask: 'Wanjiru's two containers had equal surface area. If this roof and a box also had equal surface area, would they hold the same amount?' to prepare for later volume lessons, without teaching volume now. Note the unit conventions: area in m2, never m or m3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with worked-example fading: Learners make a claim (the height of a triangular face is l), support it with their measurements, and reason using Pythagoras. A fully worked example (60 m2) is followed by a partly guided problem (80 m2), which gradually shifts responsibility to the learner and builds procedural fluency along with conceptual understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect an exit-style written response to: 'Find the roof area of a square pyramid with base 6 m, h = 4 m. Show l.' Success criteria: finds l = 5 m by Pythagoras (or states it), uses 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 15 m2 per face, multiplies by 4 to give 60 m2, writes the unit as m2, and states that the base is excluded for a roof. Check the Kajiado hall answer (80 m2). Tally how many learners still use h instead of l. Use the common errors to plan a re-teach at the start of Lesson 3, where slant height is needed again.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Each group writes on sticky notes (a) one new thing they learned (for example, 'a pyramid's triangular faces use the slant height, not the vertical height'), and (b) one new question that arose (for example, 'Does the 60 m2 roof also tell us how much space is inside?', 'If the box were a pyramid, would it hold more than the drum?', 'What will we need for a cone, which has a curved surface?'). They place the notes under the headings: 'What we have found', 'What we still need to find out'. They link at least one note to the phenomenon: surface area is only the covering material, so it cannot explain why the drum holds more than the box with the same 30,800 cm2.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes to write what you now know and what you still wonder.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups begin. Ask each group to read out one note, and cold-call 5 groups. Group the notes with the class: 'Which of these are about surface area, and which are about volume or space inside?' Point to the Eldoret photos: 'Does the pyramid roof help us explain why the drum holds more maize than the box?' Elicit that it shows how to measure covering material for flat faces, but not capacity. Highlight questions to be answered in Lessons 3 and 4 (curved surfaces) and Lessons 5 and 6 (volume). Do not answer the volume questions now; mark them as 'coming soon'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting: Learners' own questions are sorted by type (surface area vs volume, flat vs curved). Seeing how their questions relate to the anchoring phenomenon maintains a purpose for learning and shows progress, as questions about pyramids are answered while new ones point to cones, spheres and volume.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sticky notes for: (1) correct use of the terms slant height and vertical height; (2) whether learners distinguish surface area (covering) from volume (space inside); (3) whether at least one question is linked to the drum and box. Count how many groups produce a volume question, which shows readiness for Lessons 5 and 6. Note any notes that call slant height 'height' and address them in the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model (a poster or diagram) that is being built from Lesson 1 to answer the driving question. They add a 'Pyramids' section containing: a labelled sketch of a square pyramid showing h, l, half-base and the right-angled triangle; the rule 'Pyramid TSA = base area + sum of triangular faces'; the worked figures (roof 60 m2; tetrahedron about 62.35 cm2); and a note: 'Surface area tells us how much material covers a solid, not how much it holds.' In their notebooks they complete a three-column summary (What we observed, What we learned, How it helps explain the drum and the box) and write two sentences that begin: 'Wanjiru would use the slant height because...' and 'This helps explain the drum and the box because...'. They also add a 'careers' note: quantity surveyors and roofers in Kenya use these calculations to order iron sheets.
framework.teacherMoves: Display last lesson's model and say: 'What does our model say so far about the drum and the box?' (the box's SA is 30,800 cm2, found by adding the faces of its net). Then ask: 'What is new today that we should add?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds and cold-call 3 learners. As groups draw, circulate and check that l and h are labelled correctly and units are m2 or cm2. Ask: 'Where on our model do we show that the same sum-of-faces method works for prisms and pyramids?' Ask a volunteer to read the last line aloud and ask: 'Does our model explain yet why the drum holds more maize?' Guide learners to say that it does not yet, and that we need volume. Collect the notebooks' summary tables for review. Close by saying: 'Next lesson, we meet curved surfaces, and slant height will return.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with gallery review: Learners add to a single evolving model across lessons, so each new idea (slant height, sum-of-faces for pyramids) is connected to earlier ones (nets, prisms) and to the phenomenon. Writing sentence frames in their own words consolidates the explanation, and noting what is still missing (volume) creates a need for the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review the model posters and notebook summaries for: (1) correct labelling of h, l and the half-base in the right-angled triangle; (2) the correct statement of the rule and figures (60 m2; about 62.35 cm2); (3) a sentence showing that surface area differs from volume; (4) a connection to the drum and the box. Use a 3-level check (secure, nearly, not yet) and note learners who need extra support with Pythagoras or with identifying l. Plan a short starter in Lesson 3 to revisit slant height with those learners.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) How many learners used the vertical height (4 m) in their first prediction, and how many moved to the slant height (5 m) after measuring? Did the physical model make the difference clear? (2) Could learners find l by Pythagoras on their own, or did they need the right-angled triangle drawn for them? (3) Did any learners confuse roof area (4 faces, 60 m2) with the total surface area of a closed pyramid (96 m2)? How could I make the 'is there a floor?' question clearer? (4) Did learners clearly keep surface area (material) and volume (space inside) separate in their discussion? (5) Which pairs and groups participated least, and how can I involve them in Lesson 3? (6) Was the 80-minute time enough for building the nets and the practice problem? What should be adjusted next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built a square-based pyramid (base 6 m, vertical height 4 m, scale model) and a regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron, edges 6 cm). We measured the vertical height and the slant height and saw that the slant height (5 m) is longer than the vertical height (4 m). We saw that the triangular faces need the slant height.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Slant height (l) is measured along a triangular face; vertical height (h) goes straight down from the apex to the base. We can find l using Pythagoras (3² + 4² = 5²). Pyramid TSA = base area + sum of the areas of the triangular faces. The roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2, and the tetrahedron has TSA of about 62.35 cm2.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Wanjiru can use the net and sum-of-faces method to find how much iron sheet any flat-faced solid needs, and she must use the slant height for the triangular faces. Surface area only measures the covering material, not the space inside, so it cannot yet explain why the drum and box with the same 30,800 cm2 hold different amounts of maize. We need to study volume to answer that.

LESSONS.title: Surface Area of Cones and Frustums: From Sector Nets to Turkana Water Tanks
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (single lesson); extend to 80 minutes if double period
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: cone, frustum, slant height, sector, net, curved surface area, πrl, π(R+r)l, Turkana water tank, conical tank top, Pythagoras, Eldoret posho mill, drum and box

slo.purpose: Learners derive the curved surface area of a cone (πrl) from its sector net and extend it to the frustum (cone minus removed cone, π(R+r)l). They use these to calculate the sheet metal needed for a conical tank top and the Turkana frustum tank, adding curved-surface tools to the evidence for why shape and surface area are different from capacity in the drum-and-box puzzle.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) identify the slant height l and vertical height h of a cone and relate them using l² = r² + h² (building on Lesson 2: slant height vs vertical height and Pythagoras for l); (b) explain that the net of a cone's curved surface is a sector of a circle whose arc equals the circumference of the base, and derive curved SA = πrl; (c) state that total SA of a cone = πr(r + l), always saying whether the base is included; (d) derive the frustum's curved SA as big cone minus removed small cone = π(R + r)l; (e) calculate the ice-cream cone (r = 3.5 cm, l = 12 cm, curved SA = 132 cm2), the conical tank top (r = 1.4 m, l = 2 m, 8.8 m2) and the Turkana frustum (17.325 m2). Use π = 22/7.
slo.skills: Using NGSS-aligned practices: Developing and Using Models (building and unrolling a cone net, representing a frustum as a big cone minus a small cone); Analyzing and Interpreting Data (comparing measured and calculated areas); Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking (deriving and applying formulae, Pythagoras); Constructing Explanations (justifying why the sector's radius is l and not r); Engaging in Argument from Evidence (checking the frustum result two ways). Core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Communication and Collaboration; Creativity and Imagination.
slo.attitudes: Values: Responsibility (taking care of the materials and measuring carefully); Integrity (reporting measured values honestly, even when they do not match perfectly); Unity (working together in groups). PCI: Education for Sustainable Development (reusing scrap card and paper, and minimising wasted sheet metal, as a metal fabricator would). Appreciate the use of surface area calculations by artisans in real-life situations.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 gave learners the sum-of-faces method for flat-faced solids (prisms and pyramids) and the slant height idea; the box's SA of 30,800 cm2 is already established. Lesson 3 adds the first curved-surface formulae, which Lesson 4 will use for the sphere and the drum's total SA check. The lesson also introduces the Turkana frustum tank, which Lesson 6 will use for volume. For the driving question, learners see how an artisan like Wanjiru works out how much sheet is needed for round, tapering shapes, preparing them to understand why the drum's circular cross-section matters. Lesson 3 does NOT yet compute volumes or resolve the drum vs box puzzle; those come in Lessons 5 and 6.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors and cutting card: cut away from the body and keep fingers clear. Use compasses and pencil points carefully and keep them capped or stored when not in use. Do not use real sharp metal sheet in the classroom; use card or paper only. Keep walkways clear of paper off-cuts to prevent slips. Real ice-cream cones should only be handled if learners have clean hands and no allergy to the contents; a cardboard or paper cone is a safe alternative.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kiplagat's two containers each used 30,800 cm2 of Wanjiru's iron sheet, and Lesson 1 showed that the box's faces really do add up to that figure. But the drum is round, and its curved wall is not made of flat rectangles you can count. In this lesson learners study another round shape, the cone, using an ice-cream cone, a conical heap of maize or ugali flour, and the conical top of a water tank. They predict how much paper is needed to cover a cone, then cut open a paper cone to see its net: a sector of a circle (extending the net idea from Lesson 1). Measuring the sector shows that its radius is the slant height l and its arc is the base circumference, giving curved SA = πrl. Learners then use the conical tank-top data (r = 1.4 m, l = 2 m, 8.8 m2) and extend to the Turkana frustum: a big cone (R = 2.1 m, slant 3.5 m) with a small cone (r = 1.05 m, slant 1.75 m) removed, giving π(R + r)l = 17.325 m2, checked by 23.1 − 5.775. The DQB and model-building phases connect the new curved-area tools to the puzzle: SA tells us how much metal we need, and we still need volume to know the capacity.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 6 minutes.) Learners sit in groups of 4. Each group receives a cardboard or paper cone, a sheet of plain paper, and a ruler. The teacher shows an ice-cream cone (r = 3.5 cm, slant l = 12 cm) alongside a photo of the conical roof of a Maasai manyatta in Narok and the conical top of a water tank. The teacher recalls Wanjiru's problem: she must know how much sheet to cut. Individually, each learner writes in their notebook: (1) A prediction: 'If I cut the cone open along its slant edge and flatten it, what shape will the paper make?' with a sketch. (2) A guess for the sheet needed for the ice-cream cone's curved part, in cm2, with a reason. Then groups compare predictions and agree one group prediction on a mini-whiteboard or page. Typical learner predictions: a triangle, a rectangle, a circle, a half-circle, or a 'slice of pizza'. Learners are also asked to say whether they think the base should count in the 'sheet needed' and why.
framework.teacherMoves: 1) Hold up the ice-cream cone and say: 'Wanjiru made a drum and a box from the same sheet. Today we ask: how would she cover a cone? Before we do anything, I want your honest prediction.' 2) Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing, then say: 'Write your sketch first; do not look at your neighbour.' 3) Ask: 'Which part of this cone is flat and which part is curved?' and use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers; cold-call 3 learners. 4) Ask: 'In Lesson 2 we met slant height. Where is the slant height on this cone, and is it the same as the vertical height?' Wait 10 seconds, cold-call 2 learners to point it out with a ruler or finger. 5) Circulate and note, without correcting, the predicted net shapes: record tallies for 'triangle', 'rectangle', 'circle/part of circle' on the board. 6) Say: 'There is no wrong prediction today. We will keep these and test them with evidence.' Do not reveal the sector yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual commitment before group talk: writing a prediction and a sketch gives each learner a concrete idea to test, and a tally of competing predictions creates a shared reason to investigate. Linking to the flat nets from Lesson 1 (rectangles and triangles) lets learners notice that a curved surface does not obviously unroll into a familiar shape, creating productive curiosity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Learner sketches show a net shape and not just a solid; (b) learner can point to slant height versus vertical height on the cone (listen for 'l is along the sloping side'); (c) predictions include a stated reason, not only a shape. Teacher tally of predicted net shapes on the board (count how many groups say triangle, rectangle, circle part). If more than half of learners point to the vertical height when asked for slant height, plan a quick Pythagoras reminder (l² = r² + h²) from Lesson 2 before the next phase. Collect 3 sample predictions to compare later.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 12 minutes.) Station-style hands-on investigation in the same groups. Task A (cone net): Each group cuts a paper cone open along its slant edge from the base circle to the apex and flattens it. They see a sector of a circle. They measure (i) the straight edge of the sector, which is the slant height l, and (ii) the arc length using string laid along the arc, then compare it to the string length around the base circle of the cone, which is the circumference 2πr. They record in a table: r, l, arc length, base circumference. For the ice-cream cone model they use r = 3.5 cm and l = 12 cm. Task B (derivation): Using the whole circle of radius l (circumference 2πl) and the sector's arc 2πr, the group reasons that the sector is the fraction (2πr)/(2πl) = r/l of the whole circle. Area of whole circle = πl², so sector area = (r/l) × πl² = πrl. Groups then compute the ice-cream cone: curved SA = 22/7 × 3.5 × 12 = 132 cm2. Task C (frustum): The teacher shows a card cone with the top sliced off parallel to the base. Groups lay the pieces together to see that the frustum equals the big cone minus the small cone. Learners record the Turkana tank data: big cone r = 2.1 m, slant 3.5 m; small cone r = 1.05 m, slant 1.75 m. They calculate: big cone curved SA = 22/7 × 2.1 × 3.5 = 23.1 m2; small cone = 22/7 × 1.05 × 1.75 = 5.775 m2; frustum curved SA = 23.1 − 5.775 = 17.325 m2.
framework.teacherMoves: 1) Distribute scissors, string, rulers, and paper cones; remind: 'Cut away from your body, and cut only along the slant edge.' 2) Say: 'Before you cut, hold your prediction. After you flatten it, compare with the tally on the board.' 3) Circulate and ask each group: 'Which edge of the sector is the slant height? How do you know?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds; if stuck, ask: 'Where was that edge on the cone before cutting?' 4) Ask: 'How does the arc length of your sector compare with the string around the base of the cone?' Wait 10-15 seconds; cold-call 3 groups to report their two numbers. Expect close agreement with measurement error of a few mm; praise honest reporting (Integrity). 5) Draw one large sector on the board and ask: 'The sector is a fraction of a full circle of radius l. What fraction?' Wait 15 seconds, take 2 cold-calls, then write sector fraction = arc ÷ whole circumference = 2πr ÷ 2πl = r/l. 6) Ask: 'So what is the sector area?' Let groups compute (r/l) × πl² before revealing πrl. 7) Introduce the frustum with a card cone: 'Wanjiru cut the top off a Turkana tank cone. How could we find the sheet for what is left?' Wait 10 seconds, cold-call 2 learners to propose 'big minus small'. 8) Check the slant height of the small cone by asking: 'If h and r of the small cone are exactly half of the big one, what is its slant height?' (1.75 m since all lengths halve). Do not re-teach Pythagoras; just ask learners to confirm with l² = r² + h² if they want: big cone h = 2.8, r = 2.1, l = 3.5.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with a physical net and a geometric argument: unrolling the cone converts an unfamiliar curved surface into a familiar flat sector, then the fraction-of-a-circle argument (r/l of πl²) builds the formula πrl from meaning rather than memory. The frustum is treated by 'whole minus part' reasoning, a decomposition strategy that learners already practised with nets in Lesson 1. Two-way checking (direct formula and subtraction) builds confidence in the result.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learner labels the sector's straight edge as l, not r or h; (b) learner states that the arc of the sector equals the circumference of the base (2πr), with measurements within about 0.5 cm; (c) learner writes the fraction r/l or the equivalent and reaches πrl; (d) learner computes 132 cm2 for the ice-cream cone and 17.325 m2 for the frustum without mixing units (cm2 vs m2); (e) learner says 'curved' and does not add the base unless told 'total'. Use a 3-finger check: ask learners to show 1, 2, or 3 fingers for their confidence in the derivation; follow up with those showing 1 finger. Note groups that use r in place of l in the formula for the sector's radius.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 10 minutes.) Learners apply the new formulae to a design task. Task 1 (conical tank top): Wanjiru is asked to make a conical top for a tank at a school in Narok with base radius r = 1.4 m and slant l = 2 m. Learners calculate the sheet needed: curved SA = 22/7 × 1.4 × 2 = 8.8 m2. They explain in writing why the answer is a curved SA (no base is needed since the cone sits on the tank), and why l, not the vertical height, appears in the formula. Task 2 (total SA contrast): For the ice-cream cone (r = 3.5 cm, l = 12 cm), a group computes the total SA = πr(r + l) = 22/7 × 3.5 × (3.5 + 12) = 11 × 15.5 = 170.5 cm2, which is 132 + 38.5 (base circle: 22/7 × 3.5² = 38.5). Learners state clearly 'curved' versus 'total'. Task 3 (frustum formula): Learners derive π(R + r)l from the subtraction. For the Turkana frustum (R = 2.1, r = 1.05, l = 1.75), they compute 22/7 × 3.15 × 1.75 = 17.325 m2, matching the 23.1 − 5.775 result. They explain why the slant height used is 1.75 m, the length along the frustum's slanted side (not the big cone's 3.5 m and not the vertical height 1.4 m). Learners then write a 3-sentence claim-evidence-reasoning response to: 'How does the artisan use mathematics to find the sheet needed for round, tapering shapes?'
framework.teacherMoves: 1) Pose Task 1: 'Wanjiru has a roll of sheet. How many square metres does she cut for this conical top?' Give 2 minutes of silent work, then pairs compare. 2) Wait 10-15 seconds after each question; cold-call 4 learners across the room for answers and reasoning, not just numbers. Ask: 'Which measurement did you use, and why not the height?' 3) Spot-check for the common error of using h = vertical height; say: 'In the formula, l is the length down the sloping side, measured on the surface.' Use Lesson 2's slant vs vertical idea only as a pointer, not a re-teach. 4) For Task 2, say: 'Say whether your answer is curved or total, out loud, before you write the unit.' Cold-call 2 learners to distinguish 132 and 170.5 cm2. 5) For Task 3, draw the frustum cross-section and mark R = 2.1, r = 1.05, l = 1.75 on the board; ask: 'Where is the frustum's slant height on this picture?' Wait 10 seconds; cold-call 3. Then ask learners to expand 23.1 − 5.775 as π × 2.1 × 3.5 − π × 1.05 × 1.75 and show 3.5 = 2 × 1.75 and 2.1 = 2 × 1.05, so the expression becomes π(2 × 1.05 × 2 × 1.75 − 1.05 × 1.75) and then π × 1.75 × (2.1 + 1.05) = π(R + r)l. Do not rush this algebra: allow 15 seconds wait before asking, 'Why does the answer match?' 6) Close with a claim-evidence-reasoning prompt and invite 2 volunteers to share, using the sentence starter 'The artisan needs ... because ...'. 7) Link back: 'Mzee Kiplagat's drum has a curved wall too. What do you think we need to know to find its sheet? ' (Do not answer fully; Lesson 4 completes the drum's SA check.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) together with worked contrast: placing 'curved' and 'total' answers side by side (132 vs 170.5 cm2), and the frustum computed two ways (subtraction and formula), makes the role of each measurement visible. Learners explain why slant height rather than vertical height belongs in the surface formulae, tying the formulae to what the sheet metal actually covers, which connects directly to the phenomenon's central point that surface area measures material.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learner gets 8.8 m2 with correct unit and uses l = 2 m; (b) learner distinguishes curved (132 cm2) from total (170.5 cm2) and says which one a question needs; (c) learner uses 1.75 m, not 1.4 m or 3.5 m, as the frustum's slant height; (d) learner shows both methods giving 17.325 m2; (e) CER response names the formula, the measurements used, and the reason. Exit-check mini-question on a slip: 'A conical top has r = 2.1 m and l = 3.5 m. Curved SA?' Expected: 22/7 × 2.1 × 3.5 = 23.1 m2. Sort slips into 'correct', 'used h instead of l', 'forgot π or unit' piles to plan the next lesson's starter.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 6 minutes.) Learners return to the class Driving Question Board, which displays the driving question: 'Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain — and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?' Groups write new questions and findings on sticky notes or strips. Examples: 'We can now find sheet for round and tapering shapes: what about a sphere?'; 'The cone and frustum need curved SA; does the drum's wall use a similar idea?'; 'The conical top used 8.8 m2 of sheet, but how much grain would the tank hold?'; 'Does the cone with the same sheet as a cylinder hold more or less?' Learners place notes on the board under categories such as 'Surface area tools we have', 'Questions about capacity', and 'Questions about best shape'. They also mark which earlier questions have been partly answered (for example, how to cover a curved surface).
framework.teacherMoves: 1) Point to the DQB and say: 'Today we added tools for curved surfaces. What new questions do they raise for Mzee Kiplagat's puzzle?' 2) Give 2 minutes of silent writing: 'One question per note, in a full sentence.' 3) WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups to read one note aloud and say where it belongs. 4) Probe: 'Is that a question about material or about space inside? Which do we measure with surface area?' Cold-call 2 learners. 5) Sort aloud with the class: place notes on 'surface area' or 'volume/capacity' sides. Highlight that the conical tank top's 8.8 m2 tells us nothing about how much water the tank holds, so the question 'how much grain will it hold?' stays open for Lessons 5 and 6. 6) Mark one earlier note, such as 'How do we find sheet for a curved surface?', with a tick and today's date, and write 'cone: πrl; frustum: π(R + r)l' beside it. 7) Remind learners that the volume questions will not be answered today, to keep the board honest.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: sorting notes into 'material' and 'space' categories reinforces that surface area and volume are different quantities, and ticking off answered questions shows learners their own progress while keeping unanswered questions (capacity, best shape) as motivation for later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) at least one question per group is a genuine new question, not a repeat; (b) learners correctly sort notes into surface-area and volume categories (target: at least 80% of notes sorted correctly after the teacher probe); (c) learners can name one question that today's work cannot yet answer and say which quantity it needs (volume). Teacher records the number of notes in each category and flags groups that confuse sheet needed with grain held, to address in the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 6 minutes.) Learners add to their evolving class and individual models of why the drum and the box differ. Each learner updates a model page with three parts: (1) A diagram of the cone net (sector with l as radius and arc 2πr) and a frustum labelled R, r and l. (2) A short 'what we know' list: Lesson 1: the box's SA is 30,800 cm2 from the sum of faces; Lesson 2: slant height and pyramid faces; Lesson 3: curved SA of a cone = πrl and of a frustum = π(R + r)l, with data 8.8 m2 and 17.325 m2. (3) A revised 'what we still need' statement, such as 'We still need the drum's SA check (curved wall) and the volumes of all solids to explain why equal sheet gives different grain capacity.' Learners also write one sentence on how curved-surface formulae help an artisan: 'They tell Wanjiru how much sheet to buy and cut for round shapes.' Learners then complete the summary table prompts (see below) in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: 1) Say: 'Take out your model page. Add what we learned today in your own words, with a diagram.' 2) Display a sample model with blanks and let learners fill in details. Give 3 minutes of silent work. 3) Circulate and look for diagrams where the sector's straight edge is labelled l. Ask: 'Why is the radius of the sector not r?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds; cold-call 2 learners. 4) Ask: 'Does anything on your model yet explain why the drum holds more grain than the box?' Wait 15 seconds; cold-call 3. Affirm answers such as 'No, not yet: so far we only have surface area tools; we need volume.' 5) Ask a stretch question for early finishers: 'If a cone and a cylinder have the same radius, which one needs more sheet for its curved surface, if l is bigger than h?' and let them explore with numbers. 6) Close with one sentence: 'Wanjiru can now find sheet for flat faces, slanted faces, cones and frustums. Next we do spheres, composite shapes, and the drum's wall.' (Do not teach the sphere formula today.) 7) Collect model pages for a quick scan; note learners who still use h in the cone formula.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add the cone and frustum to their growing model, explicitly separating 'what we know' (surface area tools) from 'what we still need' (volume). This keeps the model honest, shows how each lesson adds evidence, and keeps the distinction between material and capacity central to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) the model page has a labelled sector with the radius marked as l and arc as 2πr; (b) the frustum is labelled with R, r and slant height l and the learner writes both methods or the formula; (c) the 'what we still need' statement correctly names volume (not more surface area) as the missing piece for the drum vs box puzzle; (d) learners cite the correct Lesson 3 values (132 cm2, 8.8 m2, 17.325 m2). Scan pages and sort into 'secure', 'needs one reminder', and 'needs re-teaching' groups; plan a 3-minute starter next lesson for the last two groups.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: (1) Did learners discover that the cone's net is a sector, or did I tell them too early? Which questions got them to see that the sector's radius is l? (2) How many learners confused l with h in the formulae, and which prompt (the slant-edge pointing in the Predict phase, or the cross-section drawing in the Explain phase) helped most? (3) Did learners keep curved SA and total SA distinct, and did anyone ask about the base without prompting? (4) Were the frustum checks (23.1 − 5.775 and π(R + r)l) understood as the same idea, or only copied? (5) Did the DQB sorting into 'material' and 'space' show that learners can separate surface area from volume, which is the core idea of the phenomenon? (6) Which learners need extra practice with units (cm2 vs m2) and with Pythagoras for l before Lesson 4 (spheres and composite solids)? Note practical issues such as scissors, string supply, and time, and adjust the cutting task (for example, pre-cut cones) if time ran short.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the curved surface of a paper cone, when cut along its slant edge and flattened, forms a sector of a circle. The straight edge of the sector equals the slant height l, and the arc length equals the circumference of the cone's base (2πr). We also observed that a frustum is a big cone with a smaller cone removed from the top, using the ice-cream cone (r = 3.5 cm, l = 12 cm), the conical tank top (r = 1.4 m, l = 2 m) and the Turkana frustum tank.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the curved surface area of a cone = πrl, and the total surface area = πr(r + l). The frustum's curved surface area = π(R + r)l, which equals the big cone minus the removed cone. We learned that the ice-cream cone has a curved SA of 132 cm2, the conical tank top needs 8.8 m2 of sheet, and the Turkana frustum needs 17.325 m2 (checked by 23.1 − 5.775). We also learned to state whether an area is curved or total and to use slant height l, not vertical height h, in these formulae.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that an artisan like Wanjiru finds the sheet needed for cones and frustums by unrolling them into sector nets and using πrl or π(R + r)l, so surface area tells us how much material covers a solid. This only measures the material, not the space inside, so we still need volume to explain why Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box, made from the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet, hold different amounts of maize.
