LESSONS.title: Surface Area of Spheres and Composite Solids: Wrapping the Football, Decomposing the Container
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes is recommended if learners make the paper-strip model)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: sphere, surface area, 4πr², hemisphere, curved surface area, composite solid, decompose, hidden face, total surface area (TSA), football, Nairobi packaging factory, drum, DQB

slo.purpose: Learners find the surface area of a sphere by wrapping a ball in paper strips and then verify with SA = 4πr². They then find the surface area of composite solids (cylinder + hemisphere, as in the Nairobi packaging factory container) by decomposing the solid into parts and removing hidden joined faces, and check the method on the drum (30,800 cm2). This moves the evidence on from 'SA is the sheet used' toward 'a sphere covers the most space for its skin'.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) state and use sphere SA = 4πr² and hemisphere curved SA = 2πr²; (b) determine the surface area of composite solids by decomposing them into familiar solids; (c) identify and leave out the faces hidden where solids are joined; (d) state clearly whether total or curved surface area is being found. (KICD ability: determine the surface area of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres, and composite solids.)
slo.skills: Measuring (circumference, diameter and radius of a football), modelling with paper strips, decomposing composite solids, computing with π = 22/7, justifying a method with evidence (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Responsibility: the learner takes care of the footballs and models used. Integrity: the learner measures and records accurately. Unity: the learner works with a team and respects each member's input. Appreciation of mathematics used by Kenyan fabricators and packaging engineers.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-3 built the sum-of-faces and curved-area methods (prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums). Lesson 4 adds the sphere and composite solids. Learners check the drum SA (30,800 cm2) with a decomposition, which confirms that surface area is only the material, and it sets up Lessons 5-6, where volume explains why the drum holds more. The sphere also supports the later claim that a sphere is the best shape of all.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep footballs, rulers and scissors off the floor so no one trips. Scissors are used for paper strips only, with the pointed end down. Use water-soluble markers. Do not throw or kick the balls in the classroom. Learners with limited mobility can take the role of recorder or checker.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kiplagat is still puzzled: the drum and the box both used 30,800 cm2 of Wanjiru's iron sheet, yet the drum holds more maize. Today learners turn to a shape with no flat faces, a football from a Kisumu school (r = 10.5 cm). They predict how many paper circles of the same radius are needed to cover it, wrap it in strips to find that the answer is about 4, and confirm SA = 4πr² = 1,386 cm2. They next meet the Nairobi packaging factory container (cylinder r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm with a hemisphere on top, no lid between), decompose it, and find that the joined circular face is hidden and must not be counted: SA = 440 + 154 + 308 = 902 cm2. Finally they re-decompose the drum (2πr² + 2πrh = 7,700 + 23,100 = 30,800 cm2) to check that the method reproduces the anchor figure, and they add new evidence to the DQB. Lesson 4 teaches only surface area; volume of the cylinder, drum and sphere is left to Lessons 5 and 6.

framework.learnerExperience: (8 min) Learners meet Wanjiru's problem again: 'A packaging factory in Nairobi wants to cover a football (r = 10.5 cm) in a thin film.' Each learner holds a football (or a ball of known radius) beside a paper circle cut with the same radius. Individually they write a prediction in their books: 'How many paper circles of radius 10.5 cm would I need to cover the whole football with no overlap?' with a reason, then sketch the covering. They guess on a sticky note (2, 3, 4, 5 or 6) and add it to a class tally on the board. They also predict: 'If I join a hemisphere on top of a cylinder, should I count the circle where they meet in the surface area?'
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the football and say: 'Last time we found the material on a cone and a frustum. A football has no flat face and no net that lies flat. How could Wanjiru find the sheet needed for it?' Give the instruction: 'Write your own prediction first. No talking for 2 minutes.' WAIT TIME 15 seconds after asking: 'Why might you need more than one circle?' Cold-call 4 learners to give their number and reason, including at least 1 who chose a low number and 1 who chose a high number. Do not say which is right. Record the tally on the board as a bar graph. Then ask: 'Is a hidden face part of the sheet metal? Raise a hand for yes, no, or not sure.' Note counts for use in the Explain Phase. Link back: 'Remember the drum and box: equal sheet, unequal grain. Keep that in mind.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Prediction with Reasoning): committing in writing to a prediction and reason before seeing evidence exposes the intuition that a sphere's skin is 'about 2 or 3 circles', so the later evidence creates a real conflict. The class tally turns private guesses into shared data that learners later test against measurements.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) every learner has a written prediction with a reason before the tally; (2) at least 3 learners mention comparing the curved ball to flat paper circles; (3) the count of learners who say the joined face is or is not part of the sheet. Note learners who say 'surface area is the space inside' and revisit the SA vs volume distinction with them. Record the tally as a baseline.

framework.learnerExperience:
(14 min) Groups of 4 collect evidence in two stations.
Station A (sphere): (1) Measure the football circumference with string and a ruler (about 66 cm) and compute the radius using C = 2πr: r = 66 ÷ (2 x 22/7) = 10.5 cm. (2) Cover half the ball with strips of paper or masking-tape strips of known width, laying them side by side without overlap, then peel them off and lay them flat. (3) Cut the strips to fit into circles of radius 10.5 cm (area πr² = 346.5 cm2) and count how many circles' worth are used (about 4). Record: strip area ÷ circle area. (4) Compute 4πr² = 4 x 22/7 x 10.5 x 10.5 = 1,386 cm2 and compare with 4 x 346.5 = 1,386 cm2.
Station B (composite solid): Using a model of the Nairobi packaging container made from a rolled-up card cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm) with a card hemisphere on top (or a drawn diagram with the dimensions), learners label the parts: curved cylinder surface, base of the cylinder, and the hemisphere. They colour-code each part. They place the hemisphere on the cylinder and identify the circle where they meet (r = 7 cm) and mark it 'hidden'. They compute each part: curved cylinder 2πrh = 2 x 22/7 x 7 x 10 = 440 cm2; base πr² = 154 cm2; hemisphere curved 2πr² = 308 cm2. They record these in a table.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Say to each group: 'Show me where you laid the strips so they do not overlap. How do you know there is no gap?' At Station A ask: 'About how many circle-areas did your strips take? Write it down before you compute anything.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds after: 'What do you notice about your number compared with our tally on the board?' At Station B ask: 'Point to the face that is covered when the hemisphere sits on the cylinder. Can the metalsmith see it? Does Wanjiru need sheet for it?' Prompt: 'Which areas did you add? Which did you leave out? Why?' Remind: 'Always say whether you are finding the total or the curved surface area.' Cold-call 3 groups to report their strip-to-circle ratio and check that they cluster near 4. For a group that gets 3 or 5, ask them to check overlaps or gaps. Rotate stations after 7 minutes. For learners who struggle, offer a pre-labelled diagram and the formula card from Lesson 3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gathering Evidence Through Physical Modelling and Data Pooling: wrapping the ball makes a curved surface measurable, so learners see 4 circle-areas as a measurement rather than a rule. Colour-coding and the hidden-face label make the decomposition concrete, building the idea that composite surface area is the sum of the visible parts only. Pooling group ratios lets learners judge measurement error and agreement.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) strips laid with no overlap or gap; (2) the group's ratio is close to 4 (accept 3.8 to 4.2) and learners say why small differences arise; (3) the hemisphere is coloured separately and the joined circle is marked hidden before any calculation; (4) the table shows 440, 154 and 308 with units cm2; (5) learners say 'curved' or 'total' when naming areas. Use a tick sheet. If more than 1 group counts the joined circle, plan a short re-model in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (12 min) Part 1 (4 min): Using the pooled data, each group writes a claim: 'The surface area of a sphere is ___ times the area of its great circle, so SA = ___.' They back it with the strip evidence and the numbers 346.5 cm2 and 1,386 cm2, and write 4πr². Part 2 (4 min): Groups complete the Nairobi container: 440 + 154 + 308 = 902 cm2 and write why the circle where the solids join (154 cm2, top of the cylinder, and the flat face of the hemisphere) is left out. They explain why the container has no lid between the cylinder and the dome. Part 3 (4 min): Groups check the method on the drum (r = 35 cm, h = 105 cm, closed): 2πr² = 7,700 cm2 for the two circular faces, 2πrh = 23,100 cm2 for the curved wall, TSA = 30,800 cm2. They compare this with the box's 30,800 cm2 from Lesson 1 and write: 'Both containers use the same sheet, so surface area does not tell us capacity.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your own data. Start your claim with: We found that...' Give each group 2 minutes of silent writing before sharing. WAIT TIME 15 seconds after asking: 'Why does 4πr² make sense when the strips took about 4 circles?' Cold-call 3 groups for the sphere claim, then 2 for the hidden-face reasoning: 'Why did the Nairobi container lose 154 cm2 at the join, in other words why is it not 440 + 154 + 154 + 308?' Ask for a revoicing: 'Who can say in other words what Group 2 said?' Contrast carefully: 'Hemisphere curved SA is 2πr², half of the sphere; check that against 308 = half of 616.' For the drum say: 'Which parts did we add? Did we include any hidden faces? Do we get the same 30,800 as Wanjiru's sheet?' Address any misconception recorded earlier: 'Is surface area the space inside?' Use the drum and box to reinforce: 'Same sheet, different grain, so what must the sheet measure? What might measure the space inside? We will come to that in Lessons 5 and 6.' Do not teach volume formulae today.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Revoicing: learners must link the pooled strip measurements (evidence) to the formula (claim) and explain why it works (reasoning). Revoicing and cold-calling spread ideas across the class. Returning to the drum SA is a Transfer Check: it shows the decomposition method reproduces a known anchor value, building trust in the method.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) claims that use measured data (e.g. 'about 4 x 346.5 = 1,386') not just the formula; (2) a correct explanation that the joined circle is hidden and not part of the outside sheet; (3) correct results 1,386, 902 and 30,800 cm2 with units; (4) learners use 'total' or 'curved' correctly; (5) at least 4 learners can explain why equal SA does not mean equal capacity. Collect a quick exit question: 'A hemisphere of r = 7 cm sits on a cylinder of r = 7 cm. Which areas do you add?' (Expected: curved cylinder + one base + curved hemisphere.) Revisit if fewer than 80% are correct.

framework.learnerExperience: (3 min) Groups revisit the DQB. Each group writes on sticky notes: (1) one thing they now know, e.g. 'A sphere's SA is 4 great circles: 1,386 cm2 for the football' or 'Hidden joined faces are not counted: 902 cm2'; and (2) one new question, e.g. 'The football and the drum have different shapes. Which holds more for the same skin?' or 'Why would a packaging engineer put a dome on a container?' or 'What is the volume of the drum, and how do we find it?' They place the notes next to older ones and move any answered question to an 'Answered' column, such as 'How do we find SA of a curved shape?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board started with Mzee Kiplagat's puzzle. What can we now add?' Ask groups to say whether their question is about surface area (material) or about volume (space inside) and place it in the matching column. WAIT TIME 10 seconds before collecting. Cold-call 3 groups to read a note aloud. Point out: 'Which questions can only be answered when we know the space inside? Lesson 5 starts with the box. Lesson 6 gives us the drum.' Highlight good questions and group like questions together. Photograph the DQB for the class record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Sorting and Tracking: separating 'surface area' questions from 'volume' questions on the board reinforces that they are different quantities. Moving answered questions shows progress, and new questions give the next lessons a purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: each group posts at least 1 'now know' note and 1 new question; at least 2 questions correctly sorted as volume questions; at least 1 question links shape to capacity (e.g. 'which shape holds the most?'). If notes only restate formulae, prompt with 'How does this help Mzee Kiplagat?'

framework.learnerExperience: (3 min) Learners update their individual class model (a flow diagram or concept map, started in Lesson 1) with a new panel titled 'Surface area is the sheet used'. They add: sphere SA = 4πr² (football 1,386 cm2); hemisphere curved SA = 2πr²; composite solids: decompose, add the visible parts only, hidden joined faces removed (Nairobi container 902 cm2); drum TSA = 30,800 cm2 = box TSA. They draw an arrow labelled 'But what about the space inside? Lessons 5 and 6' pointing to a blank 'Volume' panel. They also write a 2-sentence answer to: 'What have we learned that explains why Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box cost the same sheet?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's evidence to your model. Draw the football and the Nairobi container so we remember the hidden face.' Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model does the sheet used show up? Where will the grain show up?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners to read their 2-sentence explanation. Reinforce: 'So far our model explains the material. It cannot yet explain why the drum holds more. What do we still need?' Tell learners to bring a cylinder or box from home (e.g. a tin of beans, a milk carton) for Lesson 5, and to be ready to fill models with sand or maize.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners add each lesson's evidence to one evolving model. Showing a deliberate gap (the blank volume panel) makes the limits of current understanding visible and gives the next lessons a clear purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the models for: correct formulae and values (1,386 cm2, 902 cm2, 30,800 cm2); the hidden face noted; the arrow to volume present; a written explanation that does not mix up surface area and volume. Collect 5 models at random to spot misconceptions, and give feedback at the start of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did learners get about 4 for the strip-to-circle ratio, and could they explain differences in terms of gaps or overlaps? (2) How many groups wrongly counted the joined circle in the Nairobi container, and did the colour-coding help? (3) Did anyone use 'surface area' and 'volume' interchangeably, and what did I do about it? (4) Did cold-calling bring out learners who usually stay quiet? (5) Were the questions on the DQB moving toward volume and shape? (6) What would I change next time, for example more time at Station B, or a pre-cut hemisphere to save time? Note names of learners who need extra support with decomposing solids and plan quick practice using the Lesson 3 formulae before Lesson 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We wrapped a football (r = 10.5 cm) in strips and found the skin covered about 4 circles of radius 10.5 cm. We saw that the Nairobi container is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top, with a hidden joined circle. We added up the parts of the drum and got 30,800 cm2, the same as the box.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Sphere SA = 4πr² (football 1,386 cm2). Hemisphere curved SA = 2πr². For composite solids we decompose into familiar parts, add only the outside faces, and leave out the hidden joined faces (Nairobi container 902 cm2). Surface area is the amount of material covering a solid, not the space inside.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The drum and the box both use 30,800 cm2 of sheet, so surface area alone cannot tell Mzee Kiplagat which holds more maize. Surface area measures the material covering a solid, so we still need to find the space inside (volume) in Lessons 5 and 6 to explain why the drum holds more.

LESSONS.title: Volume of Prisms and Pyramids: How Much Maize Can the Box Hold?
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (1 double lesson or 2 x 40 minutes)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: volume, capacity, prism, pyramid, base area, vertical height, one third rule, litre, cm3, m3

slo.purpose: Learners return to Mzee Kiplagat's two containers. Lessons 1 to 4 dealt with surface area (the material covering a solid). In this lesson learners turn to volume (the space inside). They derive V = base area x height for prisms and V = 1/3 x base area x height for pyramids from sand-fill models, then compute the box volume of 322,500 cm3 and preview the drum.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) determine the volume of prisms and pyramids; (b) explain that volume (space inside, in cm3 or m3) is different from surface area (material covering, in cm2 or m2); (c) state that three pyramids fill a prism with the same base and height; (d) convert cm3 to litres (1 litre = 1,000 cm3; 1 m3 = 1,000 litres).
slo.skills: Measuring dimensions; comparing filled models; deriving a formula from evidence; calculating volume with correct units; converting between cm3, m3 and litres; arguing from evidence. NGSS-aligned practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Values: Responsibility (care for sand, water and models, and sweeping up spills) and Integrity (recording measurements and fill counts honestly). Core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (reasoning from fill evidence to a formula); Communication and Collaboration (sharing roles and results in groups). PCI: Education for Sustainable Development (reusing sand and water and not wasting materials).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 4 built the surface area evidence (box SA = 30,800 cm2, equal to the drum). Lesson 5 starts the volume evidence: learners derive the prism and pyramid rules and calculate the box volume of 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres). Lesson 6 then uses the one-third idea with cones and spheres to find the drum volume (404,250 cm3) and resolve why the drum holds more.
slo.safetyNotes: Use dry sand or water only over trays or basins. Wipe up spills immediately because wet floors cause slips. Do not throw sand. Keep sand away from eyes and wash hands afterwards. Handle card or plastic models gently and do not use cut edges carelessly. No learner should lift a full container; use small models only.

LESSONS.overview: Teacher recalls Mzee Kiplagat and Wanjiru: both containers use 30,800 cm2 of sheet, yet the drum holds more maize. Learners predict whether the box or the drum holds more and what a pyramid holds compared with a prism. In the Observe phase they fill the 5 x 4 x 3 cm and 3-4-5 triangular prism models (both 60 cm3) with sand or water and compare them. They then fill a pyramid that has the same base and height as a prism and count how many pyramid-fuls fill the prism (3). In the Explain phase they calculate the box volume (50 x 50 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres) and the pyramid roof volume (48 m3), and distinguish volume from surface area. The DQB and the class model are then updated with volume evidence, and the drum volume is left for Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners see the photograph of Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box in Eldoret. Individually (2 minutes) they write: (1) Which container will hold more maize, the box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) or the drum? Why? (2) Wanjiru says the box has a surface area of 30,800 cm2, so does that tell us how much maize it holds? (3) A pyramid and a prism have the same square base and the same vertical height. Predict how many pyramid-fuls of sand will fill the prism. They sketch the prediction in their notebooks. They share in pairs.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the photograph and say: "Mzee Kiplagat is still puzzled. Wanjiru used exactly 30,800 cm2 of sheet for each container. Today we find out what is inside, not what is outside." Ask: "Is surface area the same as the space inside?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners for their prediction on the pyramid-fuls and record every answer on the board (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 'half') without judging. Say: "Keep your prediction; the sand will tell us." Circulate and note learners who think equal sheet means equal volume.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction commitment): writing a prediction first exposes the misconception that equal surface area means equal volume and the guess about pyramids, so that learners later have to compare the sand evidence with their own ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: Does the learner write a prediction with a reason rather than leaving it blank? Does the learner use words like 'inside', 'space' or 'capacity', or still say 'size' for both surface area and volume? Tally on a class sheet how many predicted 3 pyramid-fuls. Learners who write cm2 for amount of maize need a reminder in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 with roles (measurer, filler, recorder, reporter). Station A: measure the 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm rectangular prism model and the triangular prism with 3-4-5 cm right-angled triangle ends and length 10 cm. Record base area and height or length (rectangle 5 x 4 = 20 cm2 base, height 3 cm; triangle 1/2 x 3 x 4 = 6 cm2 base, length 10 cm). Fill each model with dry sand (or water) from a measuring cylinder and record the volume: both hold 60 cm3. They compare: 'different shapes, same volume'. Station B: take an open pyramid and an open prism with the same square base and the same vertical height. Fill the pyramid and pour it into the prism, repeating and counting the number of pyramid-fuls until the prism is full. Record: 3 pyramid-fuls fill the prism. Station C: the recorder completes a table of shape, base area, height, base area x height, sand volume (and 1/3 of that for the pyramid). Groups look for patterns in the table.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and say: "Measure first, then fill. Level the sand at the rim; do not heap it." Circulate with the prompts: "Which length is the height of the prism? Which is the base?" and "Is the triangular prism's volume the same as the rectangular one? How did you check?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before helping. Remind groups to use the vertical height of the pyramid, not the slant height (as in Lesson 2). Stop one group that gets 2.5 or 3.5 pyramid-fuls and ask: "Was the sand levelled? Did you repeat it?" Cold-call 3 groups to report their number of pyramid-fuls and write all results on the board. Ask: "What do you notice about base area x height for the two 60 cm3 prisms?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection and pattern finding (investigation with a results table): learners generate their own quantitative evidence and look for a repeated pattern (base area x height = sand volume; 3 pyramids = 1 prism), which builds the formulae from evidence instead of being given them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: Learners measure the base and height correctly and compute the base area (20 cm2 and 6 cm2). Learners level the sand and repeat the fill count. The recorder's table shows 60 cm3 for both prisms and 3 pyramid-fuls. Use a checklist: correct base area (Y/N), correct height used (Y/N), pyramid count recorded (Y/N). Learners who use the slant height or the sloping edge for the pyramid are asked to find the vertical height.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole class then pairs. Learners use the table to state the rules in their own words: prism volume = base area x height (V = Ah); pyramid volume = 1/3 x base area x height because 3 pyramids fill the prism. Apply: (1) Box from Mzee Kiplagat: base 50 x 50 = 2,500 cm2; height 129 cm; V = 2,500 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres. (2) Pyramid roof from Lesson 2: base 6 m x 6 m = 36 m2; vertical height 4 m; V = 1/3 x 36 x 4 = 48 m3 = 48,000 litres of air space under the roof. They check that they used the vertical height 4 m and not the slant height 5 m. (3) Convert 322,500 cm3 to litres by dividing by 1,000. (4) Discuss in pairs: the box SA is 30,800 cm2 and its volume is 322,500 cm3. Why can these numbers not be compared? Learners write a one-sentence difference: surface area is the material covering the solid (cm2); volume is the space inside it (cm3). Preview: the drum is a cylinder, which is like a prism with a circular base, so V = base area x height should also work. Learners write down a prediction for the drum with r = 35 cm and h = 105 cm, but do not calculate it yet because that is Lesson 6.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "Using your table, what rule connects the base, the height and the sand volume?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to state the rule and 2 to explain why the pyramid has 1/3. Model the box calculation on the board, asking learners to supply each step. Ask: "Why is the unit cm3 and not cm2?" Ask: "A learner says the pyramid roof volume is 1/3 x 36 x 5. What is wrong?" (5 m is the slant height, not the vertical height.) Cold-call 2 learners to explain. Say: "Mzee Kiplagat can now tell you how many litres of maize the box holds: 322.5." Ask: "If the box and drum have the same sheet, can the surface area tell us the volume?" Give WAIT TIME and cold-call 3 pairs. Remind learners that the drum volume is for the next lesson. Do not give the drum answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with unit sense-making: learners state the rule (claim), cite the sand-fill counts and table (evidence), and justify why 1/3 and why volume units are cubic (reasoning). This builds the distinction between surface area and volume, which is central to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: Learners calculate 2,500 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 and convert to 322.5 litres correctly. Learners use h = 4 m (not 5 m) for the pyramid roof and obtain 48 m3. Learners write cm3 or m3 for volume and cm2 for area. Exit question: 'A prism has base area 40 cm2 and height 9 cm; a pyramid has the same base and height. State both volumes.' (360 cm3 and 120 cm3.) Mark each as secure, partly secure or not yet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to the class Driving Question Board. On sticky notes they write (a) a question they can now answer (e.g. 'How much maize does the box hold?') and move it to the 'answered' column with the answer 322.5 litres; (b) a new question (e.g. 'Does base area x height work for a round base like the drum?', 'Why does a pyramid hold only a third?', 'Which shape holds the most for the same sheet?'). They group their questions under headings such as 'Surface area', 'Volume' and 'Shape'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Go to the DQB. Which of our questions did the sand help us answer today?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to place a note and say why. Point to the question 'Why does the drum hold more than the box if the sheet is the same?' and say: "We know the box now. What do we still need for the drum?" Highlight the link: the drum has a circular base, and the cone-to-cylinder one-third idea is coming in Lesson 6. Add a column 'Evidence from Lesson 5' and record 'Prism V = base area x height' and 'Pyramid V = 1/3 base area x height'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: learners sort questions into answered and open, which shows what the evidence has explained and what is still needed to resolve the phenomenon, and keeps them motivated for Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: New questions refer to the drum, circles or shape (not just 'what is volume?'). Learners link their note to evidence (sand, table or calculation). Count how many learners moved at least one note to 'answered' and how many posted a new question about the drum or about equal sheet with different volume.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the phenomenon in their notebooks or on a chart. The model has two columns, 'Surface area (material, cm2)' and 'Volume (space inside, cm3)', with the drum and box in each. Learners now fill in the box: SA 30,800 cm2 and V 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres). For the drum they write SA 30,800 cm2 (equal) and V '?' with the prediction from the Explain phase. They add arrows and labels: 'prism V = Ah', 'pyramid V = 1/3 Ah', 'same SA does not mean same V'. In pairs they write a three-sentence explanation for Mzee Kiplagat of what is known now and what is still missing.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Update your model. What can you now add for the box, and what is still a question mark for the drum?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Ask: "Where in your model does the sand evidence appear?" Cold-call 3 learners to share their explanation for Mzee Kiplagat and ask the class to add one idea from each. Correct any model that mixes up cm2 and cm3. Close with: "Next lesson we use cones and spheres, and a third idea, to find the drum volume and see which container holds more."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building: learners add the volume evidence to the model begun in Lesson 1, separating surface area from volume, so the model grows toward the final explanation of why equal sheet gives unequal grain capacity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: The model shows box V = 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres) and SA 30,800 cm2 under the correct headings with correct units. The drum volume is left open or marked as a prediction. The explanation says that surface area and volume are different and that shape affects volume. Use a 3-point check: correct numbers, correct units, correct distinction.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did learners level the sand and repeat the pyramid fill, so that the 3 pyramid-fuls result was convincing? Which learners still confused vertical height with slant height or cm2 with cm3? Did any learners say that the prism and pyramid volumes were equal because of the same base? What evidence showed that learners understood why the drum volume cannot be found from its surface area? What needs to be revisited at the start of Lesson 6 (circle area with pi = 22/7, the 1/3 rule with cones) so that the drum calculation is secure?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We filled the 5 x 4 x 3 cm and 3-4-5 triangular prism models with sand and both held 60 cm3. A pyramid with the same base and height as a prism had to be filled 3 times to fill the prism. The box from Eldoret measures 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Volume of a prism = base area x height; volume of a pyramid = 1/3 x base area x height, using the vertical height. Volume is measured in cm3 or m3, and 1 litre = 1,000 cm3. The box holds 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres, and the pyramid roof encloses 48 m3.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The box and drum use the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet, but surface area only measures the material covering a solid, not the space inside. The box volume of 322,500 cm3 comes from base area x height, so equal surface area does not give equal volume. We still need the drum volume (Lesson 6) to see which container holds more maize.

LESSONS.title: Volume of Cones, Frustums and Spheres: Resolving Why the Drum Holds More Maize
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: cone volume, one-third rule, sphere volume, frustum, big cone minus small cone, capacity, litres, drum vs box, equal surface area, Mzee Kiplagat, Wanjiru

slo.purpose: Learners use matching cone and cylinder models to establish that a cone holds one third of a cylinder with the same base and height, apply V = ⅓πr²h, V = 4/3πr³ and frustum = big cone minus small cone, and use these ideas to compute the drum volume and settle why the drum holds more maize than the box of equal surface area.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) determine the volume of cones, frustums and spheres (KICD SLO on volume of solids); (b) state that V(cone) = ⅓πr²h, V(sphere) = 4/3πr³ and V(frustum) = V(big cone) - V(small cone); (c) calculate the drum volume 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) and compare it with the box volume 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres) after confirming both SAs are 30,800 cm2; (d) distinguish surface area (material covering a solid) from volume (space inside).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (matching cone and cylinder, water or sand pouring); planning and carrying out investigations; analysing data (616 cm3 vs 1,848 cm3); using mathematics and computational thinking (π = 22/7); constructing explanations; engaging in argument from evidence. Core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Communication and Collaboration; Learning to Learn.
slo.attitudes: Values: Integrity (reporting measurements and pours honestly, as Wanjiru measured and did not guess); Responsibility (conserving water or sand and tidying the work area); Unity (sharing roles in groups). PCIs: Education for Sustainable Development (no spilled water, reuse of materials); Life Skills (decision making when choosing a container shape).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 4 showed that the drum and the box each use 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet. Lesson 5 gave the box volume (322,500 cm3) and the one-third rule for pyramids. Lesson 6 supplies the missing piece: the volume formulas for round solids, so learners can finally calculate the drum volume (404,250 cm3), compare it with the box and formally resolve the phenomenon. It also prepares Lesson 7 (composite solids) and Lesson 8 (design project).
slo.safetyNotes: Use small plastic or card cone and cylinder models only. Wipe up spilled water immediately to prevent slipping, or use dry sand or maize in trays. Do not throw footballs or models in the classroom. Handle metal sheet offcuts, if used, with care because of sharp edges.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by recalling the unresolved puzzle: Wanjiru, the jua kali metalsmith in Eldoret, used exactly 30,800 cm2 of sheet for both the drum and the box, and the box volume is 322,500 cm3. What is the drum volume? They predict how many cone-fuls fill a cylinder of the same base and height, then pour water or sand with matching models (r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm) and find that 3 cone-fuls fill the cylinder: 616 cm3 vs 1,848 cm3. They derive V = ⅓πr²h, then accept V = 4/3πr³ for a sphere (football r = 10.5 cm gives 4,851 cm3) and build the frustum volume as big cone minus small cone using the Turkana water tank (11.319 m3 = 11,319 litres). Finally they compute the drum volume with V = πr²h = 404,250 cm3, compare it with the box, and explain with evidence that equal surface area does not mean equal volume. They update the DQB and the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon: Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box in Eldoret, each made by Wanjiru from 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet. They are reminded that the box holds 322,500 cm3 (Lesson 5). Individually they write: (1) a prediction of whether the drum holds more than, less than or the same as the box, with a reason; (2) how many cone-fuls of sand they think will fill a cylinder with the same radius and height; and (3) a sketch of the two models labelled 'cone' and 'cylinder'. They then share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the drum (r = 35 cm, h = 105 cm) and box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) sketches and say: 'Both used 30,800 cm2 of sheet. Lesson 5 told us the box holds 322,500 cm3. Today we find out about the drum.' Pose: 'How many cone-fuls do you think fill this cylinder if they have the same base and height?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent writing before any talk. Cold-call 4 learners for predictions, recording each on the board without judging; ask 2 of them 'What makes you think so?'. Hold up the matching cone and cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm) and say: 'Keep your prediction; the models will be our evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Think-Pair-Share: committing to written predictions exposes the intuition that equal material means equal capacity, and it gives learners a stake in the later evidence, so they notice when it confirms or contradicts their ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of learners have a written prediction and reason before sharing. Look for learners who say 'same, because the same sheet was used' (surface area/volume confusion) and note names for follow-up. Listen for whether any learner mentions 'a third' or 'half' for the cone and record the distribution of cone-ful predictions on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with roles (pourer, measurer, recorder, reporter), learners use matching hollow cone and cylinder models (r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm). They first measure and record r and h to confirm both match. They fill the cone to the brim with water (or dry sand) and pour it into the cylinder, counting cone-fuls until the cylinder is full, and repeat to check. They find 3 cone-fuls fill the cylinder. They then calculate cylinder volume = 22/7 x 7 x 7 x 12 = 1,848 cm3 and cone volume = 616 cm3, and compare. Next, learners study the football from a Kisumu school (r = 10.5 cm) and the given result V = 4/3πr³ = 4/3 x 22/7 x 10.5 x 10.5 x 10.5 = 4,851 cm3, and check the arithmetic. Finally they look at the Turkana water tank frustum: big cone r = 2.1 m, h = 2.8 m (volume 12.936 m3) and removed small cone r = 1.05 m, h = 1.4 m (volume 1.617 m3), and calculate 12.936 - 1.617 = 11.319 m3 = 11,319 litres.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate and say: 'Show me that your cone and cylinder have the same radius and the same vertical height, not slant height.' Insist on 'level to the brim' and 'no spills'. Ask each group: 'How many cone-fuls filled the cylinder? Did your second pour agree?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking 'Why do you think the answer is a whole number and not 2.5?'. Cold-call 3 groups to report their pour counts and write all results on the board; ask 'What do all groups' results have in common?'. For the sphere, ask: 'The football is 4,851 cm3. If we wrapped it in a cylinder of the same radius and height 2r, what fraction might it fill?' (hint only). For the frustum, ask: 'Which volume do we subtract, and why?' Remind learners to state units (cm3, m3, litres) and use π = 22/7. Support slower groups with a prepared table: r, h, V(cylinder), V(cone).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Table and Consensus Data: groups pool pour counts into a class table (3 cone-fuls each) so the pattern emerges from repeated independent trials, then connect it to the computed 616 cm3 and 1,848 cm3. Using one reasoning chain (big minus small) for the frustum links back to Lesson 3 and avoids a new formula to memorise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups verify matching r and h before pouring and record 3 cone-fuls. Check that 1,848 / 616 = 3 is stated unprompted. Check that recorders write units correctly (cm3 not cm2) and that the frustum subtraction uses 12.936 - 1.617 = 11.319 m3. Note groups that confuse slant height with vertical height; give a prompt card: 'Volume uses h, not l.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their groups, then as a class, to explain and apply the evidence. (1) Using 3 cones = 1 cylinder, they write V(cone) = ⅓ x πr²h and show it gives 616 cm3 for the models. (2) They compare the one-third pattern with the pyramid and prism ratio from Lesson 5. (3) They calculate the drum volume: V = πr²h = 22/7 x 35 x 35 x 105 = 22/7 x 1,225 x 105 = 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres. (4) They recall the box volume of 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres) and compute the difference: 404,250 - 322,500 = 81,750 cm3 = 81.75 litres more maize in the drum. (5) First confirming that both SAs equal 30,800 cm2, they write a 3-4 sentence explanation for Mzee Kiplagat that explains why shape, not material alone, decides capacity, using the idea that a circular cross-section encloses more area for its perimeter than a square, and they distinguish surface area (material covering) from volume (space inside). (6) They answer an extension: a conical grain heap of r = 1.4 m and h = 3 m has what volume, and how many litres? (22/7 x 1.96 x 3 x ⅓ = 6.16 m3 = 6,160 litres).
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'We have 616 cm3 and 1,848 cm3. What is the relationship, and what does it tell us about the cone formula?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to complete the sentence 'The cone holds ___ of the cylinder, so V = ___.' Then say: 'Mzee Kiplagat is waiting. Calculate the drum volume step by step. Show me πr²h with numbers.' Before comparing volumes, insist: 'First, what are the surface areas? Say them aloud.' (30,800 cm2 each). Cold-call 2 learners to state the difference in litres (81.75). Ask the key question: 'If surface area is equal, why are the volumes not equal?' and wait 10-15 seconds, then collect 3 explanations and sharpen them: 'So surface area tells us how much sheet; volume tells us how much space inside.' Challenge: 'Would Wanjiru's customer prefer a sphere? What do you think?' Use only the established idea that a sphere is best of all for a fixed surface area, without deriving it. Correct any use of 'area' for 'volume' immediately.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a number talk: the claim ('the drum holds more'), the evidence (404,250 cm3 vs 322,500 cm3 with equal 30,800 cm2), and the reasoning (surface area and volume are different quantities; shape sets capacity) is written in full sentences, which forces learners to separate the two measures and close the loop on the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each learner's CER paragraph as an exit check. Success indicators: (a) states both SAs as 30,800 cm2; (b) gives 404,250 cm3 and 322,500 cm3; (c) states 81.75 litres difference; (d) explicitly says surface area measures material and volume measures space inside; (e) uses the one-third rule correctly in the grain heap question (6.16 m3). Tally learners who still say 'same surface area so same volume' and plan a short re-teach with a quick sand pour for them.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the driving question: 'Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain — and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?' In groups they place sticky notes in two columns: 'Answered today' (e.g., 'How much does the drum hold? 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres'; 'Why does the cone hold less than the cylinder? A third') and 'New questions' (e.g., 'Would a sphere be even better?'; 'How do we combine a cylinder and a cone, like the Rift Valley silo?'; 'How would Wanjiru choose dimensions for the least sheet?').
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions can we now answer with evidence?' Ask each group to move one note and justify it. Cold-call 3 groups to read an answered question with its evidence. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds when asking: 'What new questions has today raised for you?' Invite 2 more learners to add new notes. Point out that composite solids (Lesson 7) and design (Lesson 8) will address several of the new questions, without answering them now. Praise evidence-based wording, not just correct answers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with questions-to-evidence mapping: moving questions from 'unanswered' to 'answered' with cited data makes learning visible and lets learners own the next steps in the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count how many notes were moved with a cited piece of evidence (aim for at least one per group). Check that new questions use correct vocabulary (surface area vs volume, capacity, litres). Note learners who ask design-oriented questions as signals of readiness for Lesson 7 and 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the cumulative class model of the phenomenon on chart paper. The model has: (1) a labelled drawing of the drum (r = 35 cm, h = 105 cm) and box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm); (2) the SA calculation 30,800 cm2 for both; (3) new today: the volume of the drum 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) vs the box 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres); (4) the volume formulas: cone ⅓πr²h, sphere 4/3πr³, frustum big cone minus small cone; and (5) a sentence 'Equal surface area does not mean equal volume; shape decides capacity.' They add the matching models evidence (616 and 1,848 cm3) and the football and frustum examples as supporting evidence. They then revise their original predictions in their notebooks, writing 'My earlier idea ... My new idea ... Evidence ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Build the model so that someone from another school can see the answer to Mzee Kiplagat without us explaining.' Assign each group one section of the chart. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups start so they can plan. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one part of the model to the class. Ask: 'What part of the driving question can we answer now, and what is still missing?' (Missing: combining solids and designing the best shape.) Ask 2 learners to read their revised ideas. Close with: 'Wanjiru measured, she did not guess. Tomorrow we combine solids like she does in her workshop.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Before-and-After Reflection: a model that links prediction, data, formula and conclusion lets learners see how their thinking changed, and it preserves one shared record to refine in Lessons 7 and 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that every group's model includes equal SA (30,800 cm2), both volumes, the difference of 81.75 litres and one volume formula with its evidence. Use the 'My earlier idea / new idea / evidence' entries to judge individual conceptual change. Success indicator: learners can say in their own words that surface area is the material and volume is the space inside.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners get 3 cone-fuls consistently, and did any groups' pour errors (not filled to the brim, mismatched r or h) create confusion that I used productively? (2) How many learners still treat surface area and volume as interchangeable, and which pour or sentence frame helped them? (3) Did learners connect the one-third rule to Lesson 5's pyramid ratio, or did they see it as a new, separate fact? (4) Could groups explain why the drum holds 81.75 litres more using the circular cross-section idea, or did they only quote numbers? (5) Which questions on the DQB signal readiness for composite solids in Lesson 7? Adjust the grouping and the language support for Lesson 7 accordingly.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that 3 cone-fuls of water or sand fill a cylinder with the same radius (7 cm) and height (12 cm), so the cone holds 616 cm3 and the cylinder 1,848 cm3. We also saw the football (r = 10.5 cm) hold 4,851 cm3 and the Turkana frustum tank hold 11.319 m3. The drum holds 404,250 cm3 and the box 322,500 cm3, although both used 30,800 cm2 of sheet.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that V(cone) = ⅓πr²h, V(sphere) = 4/3πr³, and V(frustum) = big cone minus small cone. We learned that surface area measures the material covering a solid, while volume measures the space inside, so they are different quantities.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained that the drum holds 81.75 litres more maize than the box because, with the same surface area of 30,800 cm2, the drum's shape (circular cross-section) encloses more space than the box's square cross-section. Shape, not only the amount of material, determines capacity, so Wanjiru can use mathematics to choose shapes that give more capacity for the same sheet.

LESSONS.title: Composite Solids: Volume, Surface Area & Real-Life Applications
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: composite solid, hemisphere, total surface area, volume, capacity, litres, decomposition, hidden face, water tank, grain silo, cost estimate

slo.purpose: Learners combine surface area (the material or paint needed to cover a solid) and volume (the capacity inside it) in one design context. They decide which quantity a question needs and use this to advance the driving question about how a Kenyan artisan designs the best solid for storage or construction.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) determine the surface area of composite solids (cylinder with hemispherical top, cylinder with cone roof); (b) determine the volume of composite solids; (c) decide whether a real-life question needs surface area (material, painting cost) or volume (capacity in litres); (d) convert m3 to litres (1 m3 = 1,000 litres); (e) appreciate the use of surface area and volume of solids in real-life situations. Key inquiry questions: How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting (decomposing a composite solid into cylinder, hemisphere, cone); using mathematics and computational thinking (multi-step calculation with pi = 22/7); constructing explanations (justifying whether a question needs SA or volume); developing and using models (revising the class model of the drum and box).
slo.attitudes: Precision and integrity in recording calculations; appreciation of how mathematics supports Kenyan water and grain projects; collaboration and respect for peers' reasoning (Core competencies: Critical thinking and Problem Solving; Communication and Collaboration. Values: Responsibility, Integrity. PCIs: Education for Sustainable Development; Life skills (decision making)).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids, and how are they applied in real-life situations such as water tanks and grain silos in Kenya?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-6 gave the formulae. Lesson 4 covered the SA of spheres and composite solids, and Lesson 6 covered the volumes of cones, frustums and spheres, which resolved why the drum holds more than the box at equal surface area. Lesson 7 uses both quantities together in the same design (a hemispherical-top tank and a Rift Valley silo). Learners must choose between SA (sheet, paint, cost) and volume (litres, grain) for each question. This prepares them to optimise and present their own container designs in Lesson 8.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep walkways clear when learners walk around the measuring stations. Use dry sand or rice only for model-filling and sweep spills at once. Handle metal tins and cardboard models carefully because edges may be sharp. No learner climbs on desks or real tanks during the field-link discussion.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret has shown that the drum and the box, each made from 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet, hold different amounts of maize (404,250 cm3 against 322,500 cm3). Now the Rift Valley cooperative asks for two real jobs: a water tank and a grain silo. Learners first predict whether painting cost and storage capacity depend on the same calculation. They then work through a hemispherical-top water tank (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 4 m, flat base) to find SA = 94.38 m2 and V = 74.844 m3 = 74,844 litres. Next they model a Rift Valley silo (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 6 m, cone roof of height 2.8 m and slant 3.5 m) to find TSA = 116.16 m2 and V = 96.096 m3. In the Explain phase learners sort questions into SA-questions and volume-questions, and justify why they are not interchangeable. They then add new entries to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise the class model in preparation for Lesson 8. All figures use pi = 22/7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the posho mill puzzle: the drum and the box each used 30,800 cm2 of sheet, yet the drum holds 404.25 litres and the box 322.5 litres. The teacher shows a photo of a cylindrical water tank with a dome top at a Rift Valley cooperative and tells the story: 'The cooperative must paint the tank and also tell farmers how many litres it holds.' Individually, learners write a prediction in their books: (1) Will the paint needed and the water held come from the same calculation? (2) Which part of the tank will need more sheet, the wall or the dome? Then they sketch the tank and label the parts they think they will need to calculate. Pairs share, then the class records a few ideas on a chart titled 'Our predictions about the tank'.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the tank photo and say: 'Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box used equal sheet but held different grain. Today a cooperative in Nakuru asks us for TWO answers about one tank: how much paint, and how much water. Write your prediction first, silently.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before any learner speaks. Then ask: 'Will paint and water come from the same calculation? Why?' Cold-call 4 learners (including at least 2 who have not volunteered) and record their reasoning verbatim on the chart without correcting. Ask 2 more learners: 'Which would you expect to be larger in number, the sheet in m2 or the capacity in m3? Can you even compare them?' Circulate and read predictions, noting who writes 'SA and volume are the same thing', and tell the class: 'We will test every prediction with evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a written, committed prediction. Writing a prediction before calculating exposes learners' conception that surface area and volume are interchangeable, and gives them something concrete to confirm or revise when the evidence arrives.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners who write a prediction with a reason instead of a blank or a one-word answer; (b) learners who use the words 'surface area' and 'volume' correctly or who confuse them; (c) the count of learners (record a tally) who predict that paint and water come from the same calculation. Use the tally later to compare with the evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners work through the Evidence Card: Tank and Silo. Station A (Water tank): a cylinder of r = 2.1 m and h = 4 m with a hemisphere on top and a flat base. Using a tin-and-ball model (or a cardboard net) they decompose the tank into the cylinder wall, the base and the hemispherical dome. They calculate: cylinder wall = 2 x 22/7 x 2.1 x 4 = 52.8 m2; base = 22/7 x 2.1 x 2.1 = 13.86 m2; hemisphere curved SA = 2 x 22/7 x 2.1 x 2.1 = 27.72 m2. Total SA = 94.38 m2. They then calculate the volume: cylinder = 22/7 x 2.1 x 2.1 x 4 = 55.44 m3; hemisphere = 2/3 x 22/7 x 2.1^3 = 19.404 m3; V = 74.844 m3 = 74,844 litres. They record that there is no flat circle between the cylinder and dome because that circle is inside the tank and is not covered with sheet. Station B (Rift Valley silo): cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 6 m, cone roof of height 2.8 m and slant 3.5 m, flat floor. Learners calculate the wall = 79.2 m2, roof = 22/7 x 2.1 x 3.5 = 23.1 m2, floor = 13.86 m2; total SA = 116.16 m2. Volume = cylinder 83.16 m3 + cone 12.936 m3 = 96.096 m3. They record every step in a two-column table (Surface Area of tank / silo; Volume of tank / silo) with units. Learners fill model silos with rice to see capacity and wrap them with paper to see covering material.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw the solid first, then split it into pieces you already know. Which faces are on the outside? Which are hidden?' Circulate to Station A and ask: 'Why is there no circle between the cylinder and the dome in your surface area?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups for their answer. Ask at Station B: 'The roof uses slant height 3.5 m. Where does the 2.8 m go?' (Check: 2.1 squared plus 2.8 squared equals 3.5 squared.) Cold-call 2 learners to say which height goes into the cone volume and which length goes into the cone's curved area. Remind groups to keep pi = 22/7 and to round only at the last step. Pause the class at the halfway point: 'Hold up fingers: how many parts does your tank SA have? (3). How many parts does your silo SA have? (3).' Collect any miscounts and re-teach quickly with the model. Ask about the units: 'Is 94.38 a number of m2 or m3? How do you know?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Decomposition and a Two-Column Evidence Table (SA vs Volume). Splitting a composite solid into known solids shows which faces count for covering and which solids count for filling. A table with units forces learners to see that the same solid yields two different quantities.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learners list exactly 3 surface pieces for the tank and 3 for the silo, excluding the hidden joining circles; (b) they use slant height 3.5 m for the roof area and vertical height 2.8 m for the cone volume; (c) correct totals: tank 94.38 m2 and 74.844 m3, silo 116.16 m2 and 96.096 m3; (d) correct units written on every line. Use a quick checklist per group; give a hint card to groups with fewer than 3 of 4 indicators.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their tables to answer a Question Sort. They receive 8 strips, e.g.: 'How many litres of water does the tank hold?'; 'How much paint is needed for the tank?'; 'How much sheet is needed for the silo roof?'; 'How many bags of maize can the silo store?'; 'What is the cost of painting the outside at KES 150 per m2?'; 'How much grain fits in the silo?'. Groups sort each strip into SURFACE AREA or VOLUME, solve at least 3 of them using their table, and write a one-line reason for each. Worked tasks: (i) Water: 74.844 m3 x 1,000 = 74,844 litres; (ii) Painting cost of the tank = 94.38 x 150 = KES 14,157 for the outer cover (state the assumption clearly that the whole 94.38 m2 is painted); (iii) Silo grain capacity = 96.096 m3 and sheet for the whole silo = 116.16 m2. Learners then return to the posho mill: they explain, in 3 sentences, why Mzee Kiplagat cannot predict capacity from sheet area alone, using the example that the drum and box have equal SA (30,800 cm2) but volumes of 404,250 cm3 and 322,500 cm3. They also compare their original predictions against the evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Read the question and underline the word that tells you what it is about: paint, sheet, cover = surface area; litres, capacity, store, fill = volume.' After groups finish, give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds and ask: 'Which strip was hardest to sort, and why?' Cold-call 4 groups to defend their sorting and invite 2 other groups to challenge: 'Do you agree? What evidence from your table supports that?' Press for the key idea: 'A bigger surface area does not tell us a bigger volume, and the drum and box prove it.' Ask: 'The silo needs 116.16 m2 of sheet and holds 96.096 m3. The tank needs 94.38 m2 and holds 74.844 m3. Which uses less sheet for each cubic metre stored? Show it.' (silo: 116.16 / 96.096 = about 1.21 m2 per m3; tank: 94.38 / 74.844 = about 1.26 m2 per m3). Note that dividing is an extension, so let strong groups explore it. Invite 3 learners to revisit the Predict chart and mark each prediction 'supported' or 'revised', with one piece of evidence for each.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a Question Sort. Learners make a claim (SA or volume), cite numbers from their tables as evidence, and give reasoning linked to the definitions. Sorting makes explicit the idea that surface area and volume answer different questions even for the same solid.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) at least 7 of 8 strips sorted correctly; (b) reasoning that names what is measured (covering material vs space inside); (c) conversion of 74.844 m3 to 74,844 litres without error; (d) a statement that equal surface area does not mean equal volume, citing the drum and box numbers. Record who needs support with m3 to litres and revisit it at the start of the next period.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the driving question displayed: 'Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain, and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?' Each pair writes one sticky note: either an answer or a new question arising from today, e.g. 'Which shape holds the most for a fixed sheet area?', 'Why does the silo have a cone on top?', 'How can we cut the cost of painting?'. They stick answers to the existing questions and move earlier questions into 'Answered', 'Partly answered' or 'New questions' columns. As a class they discuss which questions will be used in Lesson 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of our questions can we now answer with evidence from today? Walk up and move one.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 5 pairs to read their note aloud and explain which number or calculation supports it. Ask: 'What does a Kenyan metal fabricator like Wanjiru need to know before she cuts the sheet?' Elicit: capacity needed (volume), sheet available (surface area), and cost. Highlight 2 unanswered questions (e.g. the best shape for a fixed sheet) and tell the class these will shape their Lesson 8 designs. Praise notes that cite evidence, and ask the authors of vague notes to add a number or a unit.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Question Sorting. Public tracking of answered and unanswered questions makes progress visible, gives learners ownership of the inquiry, and links today's tasks directly to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: each pair posts at least 1 note; at least 3 notes refer to a specific figure (such as 94.38 m2, 74,844 litres or 96.096 m3); learners move questions to the correct column and justify the move aloud. Note learners who only restate facts and prompt them to write a 'why' or 'how' question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of 'Surface area vs volume' (poster or concept map). Pairs add a new section called 'Composite solids': a labelled sketch of the tank and silo, the pieces used for SA (wall, base, dome or roof) and the pieces used for volume (cylinder plus hemisphere or cone), and a decision rule: 'Material, paint, cost = SA (m2). Capacity, grain, water = volume (m3, litres).' They connect this to the central model of the drum and the box: equal SA 30,800 cm2 but volumes 404,250 cm3 and 322,500 cm3. Each learner then writes an 'exit statement' completing the sentence: 'To design a good container, an artisan must calculate both ___ and ___ because ___.' They also draft one idea (shape, dimensions and need) for their Lesson 8 project, such as a grain silo, water tank or sufuria for a named community.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add to our model: what new pieces did composite solids give us?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners to add one element each to the poster and invite 2 others to correct or extend. Ask: 'Where on our model do we show that surface area and volume are not interchangeable?' Check that learners link the decision rule to the posho mill numbers. Prompt: 'If the cooperative has only 100 m2 of sheet, would you check surface area first or volume first? Why?' (Always compare SA before comparing volumes.) Collect exit statements. Tell groups to bring dimensions and a community need for Lesson 8.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (concept map). Adding composite solids and a decision rule to a shared model consolidates formulae from Lessons 4 and 6 and prepares learners for the design and critique work in Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check exit statements for: (a) correct pairing of 'surface area' with material or cost and 'volume' with capacity; (b) reference to the drum and box or the tank and silo as evidence; (c) a project idea with a named community need. Sort statements into 'secure', 'nearly there' and 'needs reteaching' to plan the start of Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners correctly leave out the hidden circle where the hemisphere or cone joins the cylinder? Which learners still included it, and what model or sketch helped them most? (2) Did they choose slant height for curved area and vertical height for volume of the cone roof without prompting? (3) Could they explain, with the drum and box numbers, that equal surface area does not give equal volume? (4) How many errors came from converting m3 to litres (1 m3 = 1,000 litres) or from unit slips between m2 and m3? (5) Which DQB questions need to be carried into Lesson 8? Adjust grouping and prepare short reteaching cards for the learners who struggled.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the hemispherical-top water tank (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 4 m) has a total surface area of 94.38 m2 and a volume of 74.844 m3 (74,844 litres). We also observed that the Rift Valley silo (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 6 m with a cone roof) has a total surface area of 116.16 m2 and a volume of 96.096 m3.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a composite solid is split into known solids; for surface area we add only the outside faces (the joining circles are hidden), and for volume we add the volumes of the parts. Surface area (m2) tells us the material or paint needed, and volume (m3 or litres) tells us the capacity, so we choose the one that the question needs. 1 m3 = 1,000 litres.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explain that the drum and the box in Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill have the same surface area (30,800 cm2) but different volumes (404,250 cm3 and 322,500 cm3) because shape, not just the amount of sheet, decides capacity. A Kenyan artisan therefore calculates both surface area and volume, as for the tank and silo, to choose a shape and dimensions that give the capacity needed for the least sheet and cost.
