LESSONS.title: Project Presentations, Model Building & Unit Consolidation: Why the Drum Holds More Than the Box
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: surface area, volume, capacity, total surface area, net, slant height, cylinder, cone, frustum, sphere, composite solid, optimisation, litres, grain silo, water tank, sufuria

slo.purpose: Learners communicate and critique an optimised container design (dimensions, material, capacity) and co-construct the final DQB model that fully answers the driving question about Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the sub-strand the learner should be able to: determine the surface area of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres, and composite solids; determine the volume of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums, spheres and composite solids; apply surface area and volume of solids to real-life situations; appreciate the use of surface area and volume of solids in real-life situations. In this lesson learners consolidate Lessons 1-7: the drum and the box both have TSA 30,800 cm2, but volumes of 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) and 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres). Surface area is the material covering a solid; volume is the space inside. For a fixed surface area, shape determines capacity.
slo.skills: Communication and Collaboration: present a design with dimensions, material (TSA) and capacity, and give and receive critique. Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: check a design's calculations and decide whether a question needs surface area or volume. NGSS Practices: Constructing Explanations, Engaging in Argument from Evidence, Developing and Using Models, Communicating Information.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: reporting measurements and calculations honestly and accurately. Responsibility: caring for models and resources. Unity: respecting every group member's input. Appreciating how mathematics helps Kenyan artisans such as Wanjiru in Eldoret.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? 2. How are surface area and volume of solids applied in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson. Lessons 1-7 gave the pieces: the sum-of-faces and net method for prisms, the pyramid, cone and frustum areas, the sphere and composite SA, the volume of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres (including the drum's 404,250 cm3 against the box's 322,500 cm3), and composite modelling. Here learners use these to present their own container designs and complete the DQB with a final explanation of why equal sheet gives unequal capacity.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep walkways clear during gallery presentations. Carry models carefully. Use only blunt tools for model cutting. Do not stand on desks or chairs to hang posters. Any pouring of grain or sand is done on a tray, and spills are cleaned immediately to prevent slips.

LESSONS.overview: Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret has a drum and a box, both closed and made by Wanjiru from exactly 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet. Yet the drum (r = 35 cm, h = 105 cm) holds 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres, while the box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) holds 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres, so the drum holds 81.75 litres more maize. In this final lesson, groups present their project, a grain silo, water tank or sufuria designed for a named Kenyan community need, with dimensions, TSA and capacity. Peers critique using evidence. The class then builds the final DQB model, compares it with the Lesson 1 model, writes the Final Explanation, and links the mathematics to careers such as metal fabricator, civil engineer, architect, packaging engineer and quantity surveyor.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Lesson 1 initial model, in which many assumed equal sheet means equal grain. Individually, in 3 minutes, they write a prediction: 'Which of the group designs will hold the most for its sheet metal, and what feature of the shape will explain it?' They then pair-share and note the prediction on a sticky note. They also predict: if Wanjiru made a sphere-shaped tank from 30,800 cm2, would it hold more or less than the drum? They record a reason in one sentence.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 model and the photographs of the drum and the box. Say: 'Remember Mzee Kiplagat's puzzle. Before we present, I want your prediction, not an answer.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 learners: 'Tell us your prediction and the reason behind it.' Record 4 predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'Is anyone still thinking that equal sheet must mean equal grain? What would change your mind?' Say: 'Keep your sticky note; we will return to it at the end.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with revisiting of the initial model: committing to a prediction first makes learners aware of their prior ideas, so later evidence from the presentations creates real conceptual change instead of passive acceptance.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (a) name shape as a factor, not only material, (b) use both terms 'surface area' and 'volume' correctly and separately, and (c) give a reason with a feature such as a circular cross-section. Tally on a checklist how many still treat equal surface area as equal volume. Target: at least 20 of 40 learners give a reasoned prediction that mentions shape.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups give 4-minute project presentations (grain silo for a cooperative in Nakuru or Uasin Gishu, water tank for a Turkana or Kajiado community, or a sufuria for a school kitchen), followed by 2 minutes of critique. Each presentation states: (1) the community need, (2) dimensions, (3) the TSA of material, saying whether it is total or curved, (4) the volume converted to litres (1 m3 = 1,000 litres; 1 litre = 1,000 cm3), (5) one reason for the chosen shape. Presenters use models, posters and nets. The Rift Valley silo (116.16 m2, 96.096 m3) and the hemispherical-top tank (94.38 m2, 74.844 m3) from Lesson 7 serve as benchmark designs. Observers fill a Critique Sheet recording each group's TSA, capacity, and a litres-per-m2 of sheet figure. They check one calculation from each design independently and give 'two stars and a wish'.
framework.teacherMoves: Set the rules: 'Critique the mathematics and the design, not the person.' Run a timer. After each presentation, WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking questions. Prompt: 'Which formula did you use for the curved part, and did you include the lid or floor?' 'Did you use slant height l or vertical height h for the cone roof?' Cold-call 3 observers per presentation: 'Give one star and one wish, with the figure you checked.' Circulate and verify the arithmetic with π = 22/7. Where a group confuses surface area with volume, ask: 'Is this the material or the space inside?' Ensure that units are cm2, m2, cm3 and m3 and that rounding is done only at the final step to 2 decimal places.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery-style presentation with Evidence-Based Peer Critique (Engaging in Argument from Evidence): learners must support or challenge a design with calculations, which strengthens their command of formulae and transfers the drum-vs-box reasoning to new contexts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-point checklist per group: dimensions stated, TSA correct and labelled total or curved, volume correct and converted to litres, shape justified. Record observable indicators such as 'uses l for the curved area and h for volume', 'checks the other group's arithmetic', 'distinguishes material from capacity'. Flag groups that swap SA and V terms for immediate feedback. Expect at least 70% of groups to hit 3 of 4 indicators.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the anchor data and write the Final Explanation in groups of 4, using the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) frame. Claim: the drum holds more than the box even though both use the same sheet. Evidence: both closed containers have TSA 30,800 cm2 (drum: 2 x 22/7 x 35 x 35 + 2 x 22/7 x 35 x 105 = 7,700 + 23,100; box: 2(50 x 50) + 4(50 x 129) = 5,000 + 25,800); the drum's volume is 22/7 x 1,225 x 105 = 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres and the box's is 50 x 50 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres, a difference of 81,750 cm3 = 81.75 litres. Reasoning: surface area measures the material covering a solid and volume measures the space inside; they are different quantities. For a fixed surface area, the circular cross-section encloses more area for its perimeter than a square, so the cylinder holds more. A sphere is best of all, so artisans choose cylinders, domes and cones for a large capacity with little sheet metal, balanced against stacking and cost. Learners then apply this to their own design: could a change of shape increase capacity for the same sheet? They also state which of the two measures (SA or V) answers each of these questions: how much paint? how many sacks of maize? how much sheet for Wanjiru to buy?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now write the explanation Mzee Kiplagat can understand. Use numbers, not just words.' Give 6 minutes for writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'Why compare surface areas before comparing volumes?' and 'Which part of your reasoning says shape, not material, decides capacity?' Cold-call 5 groups to read one sentence each and have the class build the explanation sentence by sentence. Probe misconceptions: 'Two learners said bigger surface area means bigger volume; use the drum and box to test that.' Ask: 'A sphere is best of all, so why does Wanjiru not make spherical tanks for grain?' Guide them to practical needs such as stacking, flat floors, cost and welding. Check that learners do not re-derive formulae but use them as tools.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Constructing Explanations: requiring the claim to be supported by the calculated figures and a general principle pushes learners from describing a result to explaining the mechanism (shape determines capacity for fixed material), and integrates all lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Score each written explanation with a 3-level rubric: (1) states difference only; (2) cites the 30,800 cm2 and the two volumes; (3) also explains that SA and V are different quantities and that shape (circular cross-section) drives capacity. Observable indicators: correct units, correct litres conversion, no interchange of 'surface area' and 'volume', mentions the sphere as the best shape. Target: at least 75% of groups at level 2 or 3, and all learners can say which measure to use for paint or sheet versus grain.

framework.learnerExperience: The class revisits the DQB built since Lesson 1. Groups take the sticky-note questions (for example 'Does equal sheet give equal capacity?', 'Why does the drum hold more?', 'How do we calculate the sheet for a cone roof?') and move each one to a column: Answered, Partly Answered, New Question. For each Answered question, a learner attaches the evidence (lesson, formula or figure). They write 2 new questions arising from the project, such as 'Would a cylinder with a different r and h hold even more for 30,800 cm2?' or 'How do costs of welding change the best design?'. They also add a career card linking the mathematics to a metal fabricator, civil engineer, architect, packaging engineer or quantity surveyor.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board is the record of what we wondered and what we now know.' Read each question aloud. After each, WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask: 'What evidence answers this?' Cold-call 6 learners to place and justify questions. Push on partly answered ones: 'What is still missing?' Ask: 'Which career would use this mathematics tomorrow morning?' Invite a learner who has a relative in jua kali, building or manufacturing to share. Photograph the board for the class portfolio.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board sorting (Asking Questions and Defining Problems): revisiting and classifying questions makes learning progress visible, shows what evidence resolved each question, and keeps open questions for further inquiry, linking the unit back to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners cite specific evidence for answered questions (for example 'Lesson 6: drum 404,250 cm3 vs box 322,500 cm3'). Observable indicators: accurate placement of questions, at least 2 new meaningful questions per group, a career linked to the correct measure (SA for sheet or paint, V for capacity). Note learners who cannot attach evidence for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group revises its Lesson 1 initial model into a final cumulative model on poster paper. The model has four linked parts: (1) the drum and the box drawn with dimensions and nets; (2) SA = material (30,800 cm2 for both) and V = space inside (404,250 vs 322,500 cm3), clearly separated; (3) a formula toolkit from Lessons 1-7: prism TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter x length; pyramid TSA; cone curved SA = πrl and TSA = πr(r + l); frustum curved SA = π(R + r)l; sphere SA = 4πr² and V = 4/3πr³; prism/cylinder V = base area x h; pyramid/cone V = 1/3 x base area x h; frustum V = big cone minus small cone; (4) the principle: for a fixed surface area, shape determines capacity, with the circular cross-section beating the square and the sphere best of all, balanced against stacking and cost. Groups place the Lesson 1 model beside the final model and write three 'what changed in my thinking' statements. They finish by completing the Summary Table (observed, learned, explained) and revisiting their opening sticky-note prediction.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put your Lesson 1 model next to your final one. What did you believe then, and what do you know now?' Give 12 minutes for building, circulating with the prompts: 'Where does your model show the difference between material and space?' 'Where is the 81.75 litres?' 'Where does shape enter?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 groups to share their change statements. Do a class vote: 'Show with fingers: 1 = still unsure to 4 = I can explain it to Mzee Kiplagat.' Close by answering the driving question in one voice: 'Equal sheet does not mean equal grain: surface area is the material and volume is the space, and the shape decides how much space that material can enclose. Artisans use mathematics to choose the shape and dimensions.' Collect the Summary Tables.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Before-and-After Comparison (Developing and Using Models): placing the first model beside the final one makes the conceptual shift explicit, and requiring the model to include both quantities, the formula toolkit and the shape principle consolidates the unit into one coherent explanation of the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a model rubric: includes both containers with correct dimensions; separates SA (30,800 cm2) from V (404,250 vs 322,500 cm3); includes at least five correct formulae with l vs h distinguished; states the shape principle; shows 3 specific changes from Lesson 1. Observable indicators: correct units, correct litres conversions, the sphere mentioned as best, practical trade-offs mentioned. Expect at least 80% of models to meet 4 of 5 criteria. Collect exit tickets: 'Which measure would Wanjiru use to order sheet metal, and which would Mzee Kiplagat use to decide how many sacks fit?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which groups still blurred surface area and volume, and which feedback or question helped them? Did learners use the drum-vs-box evidence (30,800 cm2 equal; 404,250 vs 322,500 cm3) to justify their own design choices? How well did the peer critique stay on the mathematics? What would I change about time allocation for presentations versus the Final Explanation? Which learners showed growth between the Lesson 1 model and the final model, and what evidence supports this? Which new DQB questions could seed a future optimisation or cost-based investigation?

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Core Mathematics Grade 10 – Sub-strand 2.7 Surface Area and Volume of Solids: Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Driving question: Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain, and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction? Use what you observed and calculated in Lessons 1 to 8 to write a full explanation. Answer every section in the space under the prompt. Show your working for every calculation, use pi = 22/7, and include units (cm2, cm3, m2, m3, litres). Refer to Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret, Wanjiru the jua kali metalsmith, and your own class evidence. Remember: 1 litre = 1,000 cm3 and 1 m3 = 1,000 litres.

sections.title: Part 1: The puzzle and the box
sections.prompt: Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret has two closed containers made by Wanjiru: a cylindrical drum and a square-based box. Wanjiru says she used exactly 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet for each. (a) Explain how you can use a net to find the total surface area of a prism. (b) The box measures 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm. Calculate its total surface area and say whether it agrees with Wanjiru's figure. (c) Explain why knowing the surface area alone does not tell Mzee Kiplagat how much maize a container holds.
sections.exemplar: (a) Open the prism out into its net, find the area of every face, and add them. This gives TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length (height). (b) Base area = 50 x 50 = 2,500 cm2, so two bases = 5,000 cm2. The perimeter of the base is 4 x 50 = 200 cm, so the four side faces = 200 x 129 = 25,800 cm2. TSA = 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2. This agrees with Wanjiru's figure, so the box really used 30,800 cm2 of sheet. (c) Surface area measures the material covering a solid, while volume measures the space inside. They are different quantities, and capacity depends on volume. So two containers can have the same surface area and still hold different amounts of maize.

sections.title: Part 2: Testing the drum
sections.prompt: The drum has radius 35 cm and height 105 cm. (a) Decompose the closed drum into its parts and calculate its total surface area. Does the method reproduce Wanjiru's figure? (b) Calculate the volume of the drum and the volume of the box in cm3, then convert each to litres. (c) Which container holds more maize, and by how many litres? Does this match what Mzee Kiplagat saw?
sections.exemplar: (a) The drum is two circles plus one curved wall. 2 x pi x r2 = 2 x 22/7 x 35 x 35 = 7,700 cm2. Curved surface = 2 x pi x r x h = 2 x 22/7 x 35 x 105 = 23,100 cm2. TSA = 7,700 + 23,100 = 30,800 cm2. Yes, this is the same as the box and agrees with Wanjiru's figure. (b) Drum: V = pi x r2 x h = 22/7 x 35 x 35 x 105 = 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres. Box: V = base area x height = 2,500 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres. (c) The drum holds more: 404.25 - 322.5 = 81.75 litres more maize. This matches Mzee Kiplagat's observation that the drum holds noticeably more grain even though both used 30,800 cm2 of sheet.

sections.title: Part 3: Explaining why shape matters
sections.prompt: Use your evidence from Parts 1 and 2 to explain the main puzzle. (a) Complete this idea in your own words: 'Equal surface area does not mean equal volume because...'. (b) Using the cross-section of each container, explain why the drum's shape encloses more space than the box's shape for the same amount of sheet. (c) Of the solids you studied, which shape would hold the most for a given surface area? Explain why a sphere is not always the best choice for a real grain store.
sections.exemplar: (a) Equal surface area does not mean equal volume because surface area measures only the material covering a solid, while volume measures the space inside. The two are different quantities, so shape, not just the amount of sheet, decides capacity. Our evidence: both containers used 30,800 cm2, but the drum holds 404,250 cm3 and the box 322,500 cm3. (b) The drum has a circular cross-section of area 22/7 x 35 x 35 = 3,850 cm2, and the box has a square cross-section of area 50 x 50 = 2,500 cm2. The drum's cross-section is 1,350 cm2 larger. The box is actually taller (129 cm against 105 cm), but its extra 24 cm of height does not make up for its smaller base, so the drum's greater base area outweighs the height difference and the drum holds more maize (404,250 cm3 against 322,500 cm3). In general, a circle encloses more area than a square for the same perimeter, which is why round shapes tend to give more capacity for the same sheet. (c) A sphere is the best of all, since it encloses the most space for the least covering. In practice a sphere is hard to make from sheet metal, hard to stack and store, and costly, so artisans balance capacity against stacking and cost.

sections.title: Part 4: Surface area question or volume question?
sections.prompt: The Rift Valley cooperative wants a water tank made of a cylinder (radius 2.1 m, height 4 m, flat base) with a hemisphere on top, and a grain silo made of a cylinder (radius 2.1 m, height 6 m) with a cone roof. Mzee Kiplagat also has a pyramid roof (6 m x 6 m base, vertical height 4 m) on a small store. (a) For each of these jobs, say whether you need surface area or volume: (i) painting the tank, (ii) finding how much water the tank holds, (iii) finding how much iron sheet covers the pyramid roof (no floor), (iv) finding the space enclosed by the pyramid roof. (b) Calculate the roof sheet needed in (iii) and the volume in (iv). (c) When you find the surface area of a composite solid such as the tank, what must you do about the circle where two parts join? Why?
sections.exemplar: (a) (i) Surface area, because paint covers the outside. (ii) Volume, because capacity is the space inside. (iii) Surface area, because it is the covering material. (iv) Volume. (b) The slant height comes from Pythagoras: half the base is 3 m, so l2 = 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 25 and l = 5 m. Roof area (four triangular faces only) = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2. Volume = 1/3 x base area x vertical height = 1/3 x 36 x 4 = 48 m3. We use the vertical height for volume and the slant height for the triangular faces. (c) Decompose the solid into familiar parts and add only the outside faces. The joining circle is hidden inside the solid, so it is left out of the surface area. This is why the tank has SA = 94.38 m2 and the silo has TSA = 116.16 m2. For volume we add the volumes of the parts, giving 74.844 m3 (74,844 litres) for the tank and 96.096 m3 for the silo.

sections.title: Part 5: Using mathematics to design
sections.prompt: Answer the KICD inquiry questions using your own project or the class evidence. (a) How do we determine the surface area and volume of solids? Give at least three different solids and the formula or method you used for each. (b) How are surface area and volume applied in real life in Kenya? Describe one design for a named Kenyan community need (for example a grain silo, water tank or sufuria), say which calculation you would do for sheet or paint and which for capacity, and name one career that uses this mathematics. (c) Finally, write a short final explanation (3 to 5 sentences) answering the driving question.
sections.exemplar: (a) Prism: TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter x length, and V = base area x height. Pyramid: TSA = base area + areas of the triangular faces (using slant height l), and V = 1/3 x base area x vertical height. Cone: curved SA = pi x r x l, TSA = pi x r(r + l), and V = 1/3 x pi x r2 x h. Frustum: curved SA = pi(R + r)l, and V = big cone minus small cone. Sphere: SA = 4 x pi x r2 and V = 4/3 x pi x r3. Composite solids: split into known solids, add only the outside faces for SA, and add the volumes for V. (b) Example: a grain silo for a Rift Valley cooperative, a cylinder with a cone roof. The surface area tells the metal fabricator how much iron sheet to buy and how much paint is needed, and the volume tells how many litres or m3 of maize it stores. A metal fabricator, civil engineer, architect, packaging engineer or quantity surveyor uses both calculations to give the needed capacity for the least sheet and cost. (c) The drum and the box in Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill both used 30,800 cm2 of sheet, but the drum holds 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) and the box 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres), so the drum holds 81.75 litres more. Surface area measures the material covering a solid and volume measures the space inside, so they are different quantities. The drum's circular cross-section (3,850 cm2) is larger than the box's square cross-section (2,500 cm2), and this outweighs the box's extra height, so shape decides capacity; in general a circle encloses more area than a square for the same perimeter and a sphere is best of all. Artisans like Wanjiru use mathematics to choose shapes and dimensions that give the most capacity for the least sheet, balanced against stacking and cost.

rubric.criterion: Calculating surface area and volume correctly
rubric.excellent: Uses the correct method for each solid (prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone, sphere, composite), uses slant height and vertical height correctly, gets all values right (30,800 cm2; 404,250 cm3; 322,500 cm3) with correct units and working.
rubric.proficient: Uses mostly correct methods and gets most values right, with one or two small slips in arithmetic, units or choice of height.
rubric.developing: Confuses formulae, mixes slant and vertical height, or omits working and units, so the values are mostly incorrect.

rubric.excellent: States clearly that surface area is the material covering a solid and volume is the space inside, and correctly classifies each task as a surface area or volume question with reasons.
rubric.proficient: Distinguishes the two ideas correctly but gives limited reasons or misclassifies one task.
rubric.developing: Treats surface area and volume as the same thing or cannot say which one a task needs.

rubric.excellent: Explains why the drum holds 81.75 litres more than the box using the shared 30,800 cm2, both volumes and the cross-section areas (3,850 cm2 against 2,500 cm2), noting that the drum's larger base outweighs the box's extra height, and links to the sphere as the most efficient shape.
rubric.proficient: Explains that shape decides capacity and quotes the main numbers, but the reasoning about cross-sections is incomplete.
rubric.developing: States that the drum holds more without evidence, or suggests that equal surface area means equal volume.

rubric.criterion: Handling composite solids and real-life application
rubric.excellent: Leaves out hidden joined faces in surface area, adds the volumes of the parts, and describes a realistic Kenyan design, explaining which calculation gives sheet and which gives capacity, plus a relevant career.
rubric.proficient: Handles composite solids mostly correctly and gives a reasonable Kenyan application with some detail missing.
rubric.developing: Counts hidden faces or gives no clear real-life application.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 2.7: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why does the same amount of metal sheet make containers that hold very different amounts of grain — and how can a Kenyan artisan use mathematics to design the best solid shape for storage or construction?

lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Surface Area of Prisms: Same Metal, Different Grain
lessons.observed: We observed two closed containers at Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill in Eldoret, a cylindrical drum and a square-based box, both made from 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet and both about 1 m tall, yet the drum holds more maize. We also measured the faces of a 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm rectangular prism (TSA 94 cm2) and a 3-4-5 cm triangular prism of length 10 cm (TSA 132 cm2).
lessons.learned: The total surface area of a prism is the sum of the areas of all the faces in its net: TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length. The box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm) has TSA = 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2. Surface area measures the material covering a solid, and volume measures the space inside, so they are different quantities.
lessons.explained: Wanjiru used 30,800 cm2 of sheet for the box, which agrees with our calculation, so the same amount of material is used for both containers. But knowing the surface area does not tell us how much maize a container holds, because capacity depends on volume. We still need to find the drum's surface area and both volumes to explain why the drum holds more; this is now on our DQB.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Pyramids: Slant Height, Vertical Height and Roof Cover
lessons.observed: We built a square-based pyramid (base 6 m, vertical height 4 m, scale model) and a regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron, edges 6 cm). We measured the vertical height and the slant height and saw that the slant height (5 m) is longer than the vertical height (4 m). We saw that the triangular faces need the slant height.
lessons.learned: Slant height (l) is measured along a triangular face; vertical height (h) goes straight down from the apex to the base. We can find l using Pythagoras (3² + 4² = 5²). Pyramid TSA = base area + sum of the areas of the triangular faces. The roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2, and the tetrahedron has TSA of about 62.35 cm2.
lessons.explained: Wanjiru can use the net and sum-of-faces method to find how much iron sheet any flat-faced solid needs, and she must use the slant height for the triangular faces. Surface area only measures the covering material, not the space inside, so it cannot yet explain why the drum and box with the same 30,800 cm2 hold different amounts of maize. We need to study volume to answer that.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Cones and Frustums: From Sector Nets to Turkana Water Tanks
lessons.observed: We observed that the curved surface of a paper cone, when cut along its slant edge and flattened, forms a sector of a circle. The straight edge of the sector equals the slant height l, and the arc length equals the circumference of the cone's base (2πr). We also observed that a frustum is a big cone with a smaller cone removed from the top, using the ice-cream cone (r = 3.5 cm, l = 12 cm), the conical tank top (r = 1.4 m, l = 2 m) and the Turkana frustum tank.
lessons.learned: We learned that the curved surface area of a cone = πrl, and the total surface area = πr(r + l). The frustum's curved surface area = π(R + r)l, which equals the big cone minus the removed cone. We learned that the ice-cream cone has a curved SA of 132 cm2, the conical tank top needs 8.8 m2 of sheet, and the Turkana frustum needs 17.325 m2 (checked by 23.1 − 5.775). We also learned to state whether an area is curved or total and to use slant height l, not vertical height h, in these formulae.
lessons.explained: We can explain that an artisan like Wanjiru finds the sheet needed for cones and frustums by unrolling them into sector nets and using πrl or π(R + r)l, so surface area tells us how much material covers a solid. This only measures the material, not the space inside, so we still need volume to explain why Mzee Kiplagat's drum and box, made from the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet, hold different amounts of maize.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Spheres and Composite Solids: Wrapping the Football, Decomposing the Container
lessons.observed: We wrapped a football (r = 10.5 cm) in strips and found the skin covered about 4 circles of radius 10.5 cm. We saw that the Nairobi container is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top, with a hidden joined circle. We added up the parts of the drum and got 30,800 cm2, the same as the box.
lessons.learned: Sphere SA = 4πr² (football 1,386 cm2). Hemisphere curved SA = 2πr². For composite solids we decompose into familiar parts, add only the outside faces, and leave out the hidden joined faces (Nairobi container 902 cm2). Surface area is the amount of material covering a solid, not the space inside.
lessons.explained: The drum and the box both use 30,800 cm2 of sheet, so surface area alone cannot tell Mzee Kiplagat which holds more maize. Surface area measures the material covering a solid, so we still need to find the space inside (volume) in Lessons 5 and 6 to explain why the drum holds more.

lessons.title: Volume of Prisms and Pyramids: How Much Maize Can the Box Hold?
lessons.observed: We filled the 5 x 4 x 3 cm and 3-4-5 triangular prism models with sand and both held 60 cm3. A pyramid with the same base and height as a prism had to be filled 3 times to fill the prism. The box from Eldoret measures 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm.
lessons.learned: Volume of a prism = base area x height; volume of a pyramid = 1/3 x base area x height, using the vertical height. Volume is measured in cm3 or m3, and 1 litre = 1,000 cm3. The box holds 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres, and the pyramid roof encloses 48 m3.
lessons.explained: The box and drum use the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet, but surface area only measures the material covering a solid, not the space inside. The box volume of 322,500 cm3 comes from base area x height, so equal surface area does not give equal volume. We still need the drum volume (Lesson 6) to see which container holds more maize.

lessons.title: Volume of Cones, Frustums and Spheres: Resolving Why the Drum Holds More Maize
lessons.observed: We observed that 3 cone-fuls of water or sand fill a cylinder with the same radius (7 cm) and height (12 cm), so the cone holds 616 cm3 and the cylinder 1,848 cm3. We also saw the football (r = 10.5 cm) hold 4,851 cm3 and the Turkana frustum tank hold 11.319 m3. The drum holds 404,250 cm3 and the box 322,500 cm3, although both used 30,800 cm2 of sheet.
lessons.learned: We learned that V(cone) = ⅓πr²h, V(sphere) = 4/3πr³, and V(frustum) = big cone minus small cone. We learned that surface area measures the material covering a solid, while volume measures the space inside, so they are different quantities.
lessons.explained: We explained that the drum holds 81.75 litres more maize than the box because, with the same surface area of 30,800 cm2, the drum's shape (circular cross-section) encloses more space than the box's square cross-section. Shape, not only the amount of material, determines capacity, so Wanjiru can use mathematics to choose shapes that give more capacity for the same sheet.

lessons.title: Composite Solids: Volume, Surface Area & Real-Life Applications
lessons.observed: We observed that the hemispherical-top water tank (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 4 m) has a total surface area of 94.38 m2 and a volume of 74.844 m3 (74,844 litres). We also observed that the Rift Valley silo (cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 6 m with a cone roof) has a total surface area of 116.16 m2 and a volume of 96.096 m3.
lessons.learned: We learned that a composite solid is split into known solids; for surface area we add only the outside faces (the joining circles are hidden), and for volume we add the volumes of the parts. Surface area (m2) tells us the material or paint needed, and volume (m3 or litres) tells us the capacity, so we choose the one that the question needs. 1 m3 = 1,000 litres.
lessons.explained: We explain that the drum and the box in Mzee Kiplagat's posho mill have the same surface area (30,800 cm2) but different volumes (404,250 cm3 and 322,500 cm3) because shape, not just the amount of sheet, decides capacity. A Kenyan artisan therefore calculates both surface area and volume, as for the tank and silo, to choose a shape and dimensions that give the capacity needed for the least sheet and cost.

lessons.title: Project Presentations, Model Building & Unit Consolidation: Why the Drum Holds More Than the Box
lessons.observed: What we observed: Two closed containers made from the same 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet, a drum (r 35 cm, h 105 cm) and a box (50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm), held different amounts of maize, and the groups' own container designs showed the same pattern: the shape changed the capacity.
lessons.learned: What we learned: Surface area measures the material covering a solid and volume measures the space inside; the drum holds 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) and the box 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres), so the drum holds 81.75 litres more; we can find both for prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums, spheres and composite solids.
lessons.explained: What we can explain: For a fixed surface area, shape decides capacity because a circle encloses more area for its perimeter than a square, and a sphere is best of all, so artisans like Wanjiru use mathematics to choose shapes and dimensions that give the largest capacity for the least sheet metal, balanced against stacking and cost.
